In a paired comparison using fixed 4B checkpoints, dCoT-SFT improves over answer-only SFT by 3.56 mIoU (95% CI 3.13--4.00). The gains mainly come from change detection and object tracking, while performance drops on three appearance-matching tasks. Replacing a model's own rationale with a rationale from another task reduces mIoU by 12.2 points, showing that localization depends strongly on the reasoning context. Finally, adding GRPO with an IoU reward after dCoT-SFT gives only small and task-dependent gains, which we analyze through controlled multi-seed development experiments.

title: Diagnosing Zero-Shot Forgetting in CLIP Fine-Tuning: Attention Drift Characterizes Adaptation, Representation Drift Predicts Transfer Degradation
authors: Ruize Xia
abstract: Fine-tuning CLIP on a downstream task typically reduces its zero-shot accuracy on other tasks, and quantifying this loss ordinarily requires a labeled transfer benchmark. We study whether the loss can be anticipated from unlabeled target images that are already available during fine-tuning. Four signals are compared: the entropy of CLS token attention, linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) with the pretrained model, embedding drift, and relative weight change. ViT-B/32 is adapted by full fine-tuning (Full FT) and by LoRA on EuroSAT and Oxford-IIIT Pets over four learning rates and three seeds, with an additional ViT-B/16 grid; DTD and GTSRB are held out as confirmation targets, and forgetting is measured as zero-shot retention on CIFAR-100, Food-101, and ImageNet-R. Within a fixed configuration, the change in attention entropy is strongly associated with forgetting (mean $|\rho|=0.860$). Its sign, however, depends on the dataset, the adaptation method, and the backbone, and the pooled correlation falls to 0.361. A block decomposition shows that this sign is determined almost entirely by blocks 7 to 12. CKA ranks runs by retention at $\rho=0.960$, and the ranking is already established after the first of six epochs ($\rho=0.959$). On the held-out targets, CKA reaches $\rho=0.95$, and the block account correctly predicts the sign of the attention change for both datasets. These results support a simple decision rule: CKA is suited to comparisons across configurations, whereas attention entropy is informative only within a single configuration. The evidence is limited to one model family and short training schedules.

title: Out-of-distribution AI-generated image detection with zero-phase deconvolution for residual whitening
authors: Yusuf Yigit Pilavc{\i} (UNICAEN, GREYC), Antoine Mallet (CRIStAL), Vincent Itier (IMT Nord Europe, CRIStAL, CERI SN - IMT Nord Europe), Jan Butora (CRIStAL), J\'er\'emie Boulanger (CRIStAL), Patrick Bas (CRIStAL)
abstract: Current AI-generated image detection methods struggle in out-of-distribution testing conditions because detectors are usually not robust when evaluated on generators not included in the training set. This work explores a way to mitigate the forensic bias between sources of images -whether real or generated -by removing generator-specific fingerprints. This new training process can be approximated by pre-processing involving a deconvolution operation designed to remove correlated noise patterns inducing loss of generalization. Indeed, we show that whitening the spatial distribution of the image noise residuals can significantly improve the performance of detectors on images coming from generators unseen during training. In particular, an end-to-end CNN model trained on whitened image residuals improves detection by 12.6% on average compared to a training involving original images.

title: Background Bias Assessment and Mitigation in Plant Disease Detection Using EfficientNet-B0 with Image Processing
authors: Majed Molhi, Nishi Gupta, Ali Algumaei
abstract: Plant disease detection using deep learning has achieved remarkable accuracies exceeding 99% on benchmark datasets. However, these metrics may mask a critical vulnerability: models may be taking advantage of false background correlations instead of learning real pathological features. This study presents a systematic investigation of background bias in plant disease detection through a two-stage training framework with quantitative validation. We propose a three-condition evaluation protocol testing models on original, leaf-only, and background-only images to directly measure background dependency. Our approach combines standard transfer learning using EfficientNet-B0 and manipulation of background information during optimization. Experimental results on the PlantVillage dataset (20,638 images, 15 disease classes) show that while our model achieves 98.97% accuracy on the original images and maintains 96.62% accuracy on leaf-only images, the performance drops to 23.58% on background-only images. The calculated background bias (BBC) coefficient of 0.762 indicates that a large part of the model's predictive performance depends on leaf-related features rather than background distortions. This research offers clear evidence that even with the most advanced models, environmental shortcuts can be leveraged, and this highlights the importance of bias evaluation. The approach that has been used has laid a foundation for the development of agricultural AI that is ready for deployment. The implementation, models, and evaluation process are all publicly available.

title: ReactionBench: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Modeling Reactions to Video
authors: Yibo Zhao, Ao Qu, Xuan Jiang, Jiahao Xu, Keane Ong, Hang Jiang, Zhaofeng Wu, Dingyi Zhuang, Yihong Tang, Kaichen Zhou, Jinhua Zhao, Paul Pu Liang
abstract: Understanding what happens in a video is not sufficient for socially responsive multimodal systems: such systems also aim to relate what a person observes to how that person responds. Existing video benchmarks largely evaluate events, temporal reasoning, or people depicted in the video, while affective and viewer-response datasets often focus on emotion labels, aggregate responses, or prediction from the stimulus alone. This leaves an underexplored question: can current multimodal models ground an observed viewer reaction in the stimulus context associated with it? We introduce ReactionBench, a human-anchored benchmark for reaction-specific video understanding. Built from a candidate pool of 31,834 synchronized stimulus-reaction clips spanning 433 hours and eight domains, ReactionBench evaluates three complementary abilities: ranking the intensity of a viewer's reactions within a video, matching a reaction to its temporally aligned stimulus, and explaining the concrete stimulus cues linked to that reaction. Human annotation provides 14,894 ratings over 3,257 moments, and the frozen evaluation comprises 250 intensity profiles, 112 matching items, and 200 rationale items with 447 blind-written human references. Across seven multimodal models, reaction-specific grounding remains challenging: the best model reaches 50.9% accuracy on four-way stimulus-reaction matching, while GPT-5 shows no detectable loss under reaction substitution. Performance is also sensitive to evaluation protocol. Project page: https://yibozh.github.io/ReactionBench-page/

title: SIMIT: Self-Improving Vision-Language Models via Imagination at Test-Time
authors: Mehmet Onurcan Kaya, Desmond Elliott, Dim P. Papadopoulos
abstract: We introduce SIMIT, a test-time self-improvement framework in which a vision-language model creates its own query-specific training data before answering an unlabeled test query. Our goal is to improve performance on a given target test set without annotations or external models. To pursue this goal, some test-time methods improve answers through longer reasoning or repeated sampling but leave the model unchanged. Others update the model using rewards based on majority agreement among multiple candidate answers or the model's own judgments of correctness, but such rewards can reinforce existing mistakes. SIMIT instead imagines similar problems whose solutions it controls: a model need not correctly solve the target query to construct useful practice examples. It synthesizes diverse (question, answer, image) triplets by specifying each answer before realizing its image. To support diverse multimodal tasks, SIMIT combines native image generation with an extensible skill library for structured visuals, including documents, charts, and diagrams. Within this pipeline, multi-stage verification checks that images support their assigned answers, while difficulty filtering retains informative examples. Adaptive budgeting further targets this practice by allocating more samples to queries the model is less confident in answering. The resulting data can improve the model in-context (SIMIT-ICL) or in-weight (SIMIT-FT). Across 17 diverse benchmarks, SIMIT outperforms existing self-improvement methods. Its best configuration achieves a +7.20% mean relative gain over BAGEL-7B, while training-free SIMIT-ICL achieves +6.98%.

title: Auditing GeoFM Evaluation for Field-Extent Segmentation: Label Proxies, Baselines, and When Frozen Features Match Fine-tuning
authors: Santosh Pant
abstract: Geospatial foundation-model (GeoFM) benchmarks for agricultural field-extent segmentation often rely on cropland land-cover proxies and compare against per-pixel spectral baselines. We measure how these choices affect conclusions using identical single-date Sentinel-2 pixels from six countries. Replacing polygon-derived field labels with ESA WorldCover cropland raises random-forest AUROC from 0.55-0.82 to 0.79-0.96, showing that the proxy creates a more spectrally separable task. On the actual field-extent labels, a from-scratch U-Net reaches 0.89-0.98 AUROC and has higher point AUROC than a Prithvi frozen linear probe in five of six regions. We then compare a frozen backbone and full fine-tuning using the same decoder for Prithvi and TerraMind, with ten matched seeds. At $\varepsilon=0.02$ AUROC, 9 of 12 region$\times$model cells are TOST-equivalent. Kenya is the common failure case: positives cover roughly 0.1% of pixels, and full fine-tuning performs better for both models. Cross-region results are less favorable to frozen models. On AUROC and average precision (AP), the U-Net leads the full 30-transfer matrix, while an exploratory analysis excluding Kenya finds that both frozen decoders outperform their fine-tuned counterparts; no AUROC difference is detected between frozen TerraMind and the U-Net in that subset. For Prithvi, a frozen decoder trains about $110\times$ fewer parameters than full fine-tuning. These results argue for auditing labels and baselines before interpreting GeoFM rankings, and for testing a frozen decoder before assuming that full fine-tuning will help. Our conclusions are limited to single-date, per-pixel field-extent segmentation, not parcel-boundary or instance delineation.

title: SemaNorm: Stain Normalization via Semantic and Morphology Alignment for Robust Cross-Hospital Computational Pathology
authors: Subhankar Chattoraj, Sawon Pratiher, Arijit Ghosh, Prashant Khare, Writankar Kundu, Karan Vishwakarma, Preha Handa, Kirti Rashmi, Hubert Konik
abstract: Stain variability remains a major source of domain shift in computational pathology, yet existing normalization methods largely optimize color consistency without explicitly preserving morphology or diagnostic semantics. We propose SemaNorm, a self-supervised stain canonicalization stain normalizer to recover clean patches from strongly perturbed inputs, avoiding paired transfer, adversarial instability, and identity collapse. It further combines a frozen pathology foundation-model consistency loss with a differentiable nuclei-structure loss to preserve semantic and cellular organization. SemaNorm is evaluated across Camelyon17-WILDS and NCT-CRC-HE-100K using cross-hospital tumor classification, cell-graph morphology metrics, and semantic stability measured with an independent held-out foundation encoder. SemaNorm improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 5.9% over the strongest normalization baseline and by 13.5% over no normalization, while achieving the best morphology preservation. Independent foundation-model and cell-graph analyses further confirm improved semantic and structural stability. These results establish morphology- and semantics-aware optimization as a principled alternative to color-only stain normalization.

title: Memorix: Managing Memory Selections for AI Agents
authors: Jing Zhang, Xiaguannan Song, Dong Du, Erhu Feng, Yubin Xia
abstract: AI agents now handle a growing share of tasks across sessions within a persistent project. Their behavior depends not only on the model, but heavily on the persistent state they read from the environment. Existing systems assemble this memory at use time, splicing selected files into the prompt as a one-off payload. As a result, per-task assembly is costly and can still miss critical material, failures cannot be traced or replayed, and agents can read documentation written for the wrong version. Our key insight is that what an agent should read is mostly determined by its project, so the selection can be computed once, ahead of time, and reused across tasks. We propose Memorix, an agent memory system that realizes this insight. Memorix achieves this via three key mechanisms: (1) an immutable and versioned Store pins every source by identity and reproduces historical layouts cheaply, (2) a View that splits selection (Derivations) from composition (Environment), making the result reproducible and shareable, and (3) Quests and Profiles keep a delivered view refreshable and available inside the project as sources evolve. We implement Memorix and evaluate it on SWE-ContextBench and LibEvolutionEval against mainstream agent memory systems. Precomputed Environments raise resolved rate by up to 1.5X and deliver the correct library version on every version-conditioned task, while cutting amortized cost by up to 100X and build time by up to 38X.

title: DDEL: Closed-Loop Mutual Enhancement of Dataset Distillation and Ensemble Learning
authors: Weiqi Zhang, Yongquan Yang
abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) reduces a training set to a small set of examples, while ensemble learning (EL) combines predictions from several models. When applied in sequence, the distilled set remains fixed as the ensemble learns. We introduce DDEL, a framework that feeds ensemble behavior back into distillation. Each round trains the ensemble, measures loss and prediction disagreement on the source data, and uses these signals to guide the next data update. We implement this loop with distribution matching and a homogeneous three-member ensemble. Preliminary experiments cover skin lesion classification (ISIC 2019), treatment-response prediction (I-SPY1), and binary two-year prognosis classification (NSCLC-Radiomics). With the same images-per-class budget as the open-loop comparison, DDEL reaches balanced accuracy 0.3471 on ISIC and mean ROC-AUC 0.5120 and 0.5597 on I-SPY1 and NSCLC. The I-SPY1 difference is small, and the ISIC trajectory shows that more rounds do not consistently improve performance. These results offer initial evidence for studying DD-EL feedback, with its computational cost and robustness still requiring controlled evaluation.

title: CarDiff: Anatomically Aware Dental Caries Synthesis using Diffusion
authors: Sanyam Jain, Bruna Neves de Freitas, Alexandros Iosifidis, Ruben Pauwels
abstract: Synthetic medical image generation can help address limited annotated data in dental imaging, particularly for under-represented caries classes. In this work, we present CarDiff, a semi-supervised framework for dental caries synthesis in panoramic radiographs. The method combines paired mask-image learning with self-supervised generation from augmented masks, while incorporating anatomy-aware conditioning between lesion regions and surrounding structures. Semantic consistency is enforced through segmentation-guided supervision and adversarial anatomical alignment. Experiments on the MLUA-DC1000 dataset show that CarDiff achieves improved synthesis quality compared with existing semantic synthesis baselines, obtaining the best Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) (90.76) and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) (0.48) scores among evaluated methods. We further assess the generated radiographs for downstream segmentation augmentation across seven architectures. Using a 5x augmented training set improves average Dice score by up to 6.5%, with larger gains observed for medium and combined lesion classes. These results suggest that anatomically consistent diffusion synthesis may be useful for dental radiograph augmentation under limited supervision. The code is available at https://github.com/s4nyam/CarDiff.

title: SAMP: Self-Adaptive Margin Prioritization For Robust Diffusion Watermarking
authors: Yuhao Xue, Jiuan Zhou, Yu Cheng, Zhaoxia Yin
abstract: Diffusion models have made high-fidelity visual generation widely accessible, while also lowering the barrier to producing convincing visual forgeries and complicating content provenance. Existing watermarking methods typically use a fixed embedding strength throughout denoising or treat all watermark dimensions equally. As a result, they may introduce unnecessary distortion when some watermark dimensions are already reliable, while failing to sufficiently reinforce those that are more vulnerable to subsequent perturbations. Therefore, robust watermarking requires adapting both the embedding strength during denoising and the optimization priority across watermark dimensions. To address this problem, we present SAMP, a self-adaptive framework consisting of global margin regulation and vulnerability-sensitive allocation. Global margin regulation adjusts the embedding strength according to the separation between the target codeword and competing codewords, together with the estimated effects of common attacks. Vulnerability-sensitive allocation identifies watermark dimensions that are more easily weakened by local perturbations and gives them higher optimization priority. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMP achieves an average information recovery accuracy of 0.993. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, SAMP improves PSNR by 16.8% and reduces LPIPS by 47.1%. These results validate the effectiveness of SAMP for reliable and high-quality diffusion watermarking.

title: CRaFT-XDet: Causal and Robust Fusion Transformer for Dual-Energy X-ray Prohibited Item Detection
authors: Moinul Hossain, Munshaibur Rahman Mahin, Taskin Khaleque, Mohammad Sakib Mahmood, M. F. Mridha, Md. Jakir Hossen
abstract: Automated prohibited item detection in X-ray security imagery is fundamentally constrained by severe object overlap, scanner-dependent domain shifts, and spurious correlations induced by cluttered baggage composition. Existing detectors largely rely on appearance-driven supervision, limiting their robustness and cross-scanner generalisation. We introduce CRaFT-XDet, a causality-grounded and physics- motivated detection framework that reformulates X-ray threat detection as invariant representation learning under attenuation-driven modality variation. Our approach is grounded in a Scanner-Invariant Causal Detection formalisation (Theorem 1), which establishes that minimising the proposed Causal Invariance Regularisation (CIR) objective across partitioned scanner environments approximates the interventional distribution P (Y | do(Xobj)) under standard identifiability assumptions, providing a principled causal formulation for dual-energy X-ray detection. CRaFT-XDet integrates: (i) causal feature disentanglement to suppress context-induced shortcuts; (ii) physics-motivated regularisation to enforce material-consistent embeddings; and (iii) transformer-based cross-energy interaction modelling for structured reasoning in cluttered scenes. With 29.2 M parameters, 89.5 GFLOPs, and 345 FPS (1.7 ms inference), CRaFT-XDet is real-time deployable. Trained on SIXray with five-fold cross-validation, the framework achieves 0.9389 mAP@0.5 and 0.8021 mAP@0.5:0.95. Without domain adaptation, CRaFT-XDet maintains strong cross- dataset performance on OPIXray and HiXray, indicating robust generalization across heterogeneous scanner distributions. In category-agnostic binary threat detection, the model attains 93.92% recall and 0.9031 mean IoU, highlighting reliability in safety-critical screening where missed detections are costly.

title: When frequency domain classification is superior to spatial
authors: Yanir Harel, Shalom Rosner, Ronit D. Gross, Tal Halevi, Shilo Glam, Ella Koresh, Ido Kanter
abstract: Modern image classification models largely rely on local characteristics and feature extraction for their predictions. This focused approach works well in the spatial domain, but reportedly falls short in the frequency domain, even though both representations contain the same information. This study demonstrates that the significant reduction in accuracy in the frequency domain stems from the lack of local features. Locally swapping data in the frequency domain significantly decreases its inverse spatial domain accuracy, even below that of the frequency domain; however, the frequency domain accuracy remains relatively constant. Moreover, the use of datasets containing global features in the spatial domain yields higher accuracy in the frequency domain. Using these results, a hybrid model is constructed, combining one model trained only in the frequency domain and another trained only in the spatial domain to achieve higher classification accuracy. The proposed visual geometry group (VGG) and vision transformer (ViT) architectures are trained on the ImageNet-100, WikiArt, DTD, FMD, PSVRT, and KTH-TIPS2-b datasets and evaluated.

title: CRAFT: Corrective and Robust Multi-Agent Framework for Text-to-Parametric CAD
authors: Mohammed Musthafa Rafi, Anushrut Jignasu, Mahdi Saraeian, Chinmay Hegde, Aditya Balu, Adarsh Krishnamurthy
abstract: Text-to-CAD generation has the potential to make mechanical CAD more accessible, but existing approaches face a trade-off between data dependence and output fidelity. Supervised methods rely on large paired text-model datasets, while zero-shot prompting strategies are often brittle and tend to lose the parametric structure needed for downstream editing and customization. We present CRAFT, a corrective and robust multi-agent framework that produces parametric OpenSCAD programs from natural language without task-specific training. At its core is a JSON intermediate representation that carries symbolic parametric expressions throughout the generation process, so the resulting models remain editable and retain their parametric structure. CRAFT combines semantic understanding, parametric planning, compilation, rendering, self-correction, and component-level verification within a layered recovery process, using multi-view visual feedback to detect and repair geometric errors. Across NopSCADlib, ABC, and Slice-100K, CRAFT is competitive with direct zero-shot baselines in perceptual and geometric quality while exposing substantially more editable parametric structure.

title: From Zero to OCR: A Data-Centric Framework for Unsupported Low-Resource Scripts
authors: Faizan Iqbal, Haq Nawaz Malik, Hafsah Pervaiz
abstract: Optical character recognition (OCR) remains inaccessible to many low-resource scripts because annotated document images are unavailable and synthetic training data can fail to preserve script-specific visual structure. We present a data-centric framework that builds end-to-end OCR for such scripts from only an unannotated text corpus and digital fonts, without manually annotating a single training image. A synthetic data engine renders word, line and page images with correct complex-script shaping and automatically derived labels; a YOLOv8 word detector and a convolutional recurrent recognizer trained with connectionist temporal classification learn from these images; and a stage-gate evaluation protocol isolates recognition error before detection is introduced. We demonstrate the framework on Kashmiri, a Perso-Arabic Nastaliq script with approximately 6.8 million speakers that none of six widely used OCR engines supports. Three line-level recognizers, including one transferred from Arabic, stalled between 41% and 79% character error rate (CER), motivating a word-level formulation; subsequent improvements came primarily from rendering fidelity, diacritic-preserving crop margins and tuned non-maximum suppression. The resulting system achieves 0.39% CER on held-out words, 10.0% on synthetic pages and 13.5% on browser-rendered digital pages, and establishes reference results of 18.45% on typeset book pages and 49.8% on degraded historical documents. We publicly release the trained models, the inference code and a synthetic dataset of 285,864 Kashmiri text-line images, and we describe a step-by-step procedure for building OCR for other unsupported scripts.

title: HistGramBench: Measuring Structural Recovery When Multimodal Models Redraw Historical Mathematical Diagrams as TikZ
authors: Minh Quang Tran, Carter He, Cameron Bloch, Zitai Huang, Thien Truong Vo, Trong Nguyen Tran, Isaac Chen
abstract: Digital libraries preserve mathematical books printed from the sixteenth to the twentieth century, but the lettered diagrams in them, the figures on which Euclidean proofs depend, remain scanned images whose content cannot be searched. Redrawing such a diagram as a short drawing program would record which points lie on which lines and circles. But a printed plate offers no source code against which the redrawing could be checked. We introduce HistGramBench, a benchmark of 2,507 diagrams from 95 works printed between 1551 and 1933 in eight languages. For each diagram, two AI models from different providers agree on the facts a reader takes from the figure, such as which lines are parallel or where two lines meet, and every redrawing is checked against those facts on the model's own drawing. We evaluate six affordable AI models. The best recovers about three fifths of these facts, and most of what the models miss comes from programs that never produce a drawing. Parallels and tangencies are the hardest relations to reproduce. HistGramBench gives historians and librarians a way to measure when such tools can make old mathematical diagrams searchable.

title: AdaptAD: Foundation Model Adaptation with Missing Modality Robustness for Alzheimer's Disease Staging Across the Disease Continuum
authors: Dawa Chyophel Lepcha, Sophie A. Martin, Pierrick Coup\'e, Shabbir Syed Abdul
abstract: Staging Alzheimer's disease (AD) across its continuum, from cognitively normal (CN) through mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia from a single structural MRI remains difficult because 3-D networks overfit small cohorts, and FreeSurfer morphometry is often unavailable. We present AdaptAD, which reads a registered T1-weighted scan as 16 anatomically placed 2.5-D slices through the medial temporal lobe and adapts a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), training 3.5 M of 89 M parameters. Morphometry enters as tokens when present, or as a learned [MISSING] token, and a missing-aware stacker fuses both experts. Under a pre-registered protocol, ten methods were compared for three-class CN/MCI/AD staging on identical 5-fold splits of 597 ADNI participants, 29% without FreeSurfer, with Holm-corrected paired bootstrap tests. The locked model was tested once on 993 OASIS-3 participants (988 scored by every method). On ADNI, AdaptAD achieved a three-class macro-AUC of 0.745 (95% CI 0.709 to 0.781), ranking first and significantly exceeding full fine-tuning, ShaSpec and a 3-D CNN. On OASIS-3 it reached 0.780 (0.748 to 0.814), and on the CDR-based label (0.804) it significantly outperformed every 3-D and image-tabular method. LoRA matched full fine-tuning with 25 times fewer trainable parameters, and removing morphometry changed external macro-AUC by less than 0.003. The disease score tracked MMSE and CDR-SB within diagnostic groups and stratified MCI-to-dementia progression (log-rank p < 0.001), while saliency concentrated in medial temporal and periventricular regions. A parameter-efficient 2-D foundation model can therefore stage the full AD continuum from a routine T1 scan without morphometry, offering a scalable route to memory-clinic deployment.

title: SCRAMJet: An Ultra Low Latency JetClass-Scale Transformer for the HL-LHC Level-1 Trigger
authors: Aadeesh Sharma, Chang Sun, Lauri Laatu, Arianna Cox, Benedikt Maier, Alexander Tapper, Maria Spiropulu, Wayne Luk, Zhiqiang Que
abstract: Level-1 Triggers at the LHC classify collisions within a few microseconds on FPGAs, where a network is a fully unrolled circuit whose cost is area rather than time. We present SCRAMJet, a transformer encoder that replaces multi-head attention with a low-rank projection, trains under per-parameter learned fixed-point quantization, and compiles to Verilog with distributed arithmetic optimization. On the ten-class JetClass dataset it reaches $71.4 \pm 0.6\%$ accuracy with 0.157M multiply-accumulates, 6.1 accuracy points above the strongest published resource-constrained model at an eighth of the operations, and meets timing on a Virtex UltraScale+ VU13P at 147 ns using 25.7% of the logic. We also show that resource-aware training silently removes attention channels: one whose learned bit-width reaches zero still carries signal during training but is absent from the compiled circuit, so the loss never sees it go. We call these virtual channels, and a floor on the attention datalane that prevents them is worth 3.1 accuracy points at matched budget. Code and trained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Aaddy-1/hgq-jetformer.

title: Evaluating Context Sensitivity of Collaboration Behavior in Multi Party Simulation Frameworks
authors: Anvesh Rao Vijjini, Sheshera Mysore, Pegah Jandaghi, Ashish Sharma, Snigdha Chaturvedi, Bahareh Sarrafzadeh
abstract: Group Social Behavior is increasingly used as a lens to study Large language model (LLM) simulations to aid model training and evaluation. However, little prior work has examined how contextual factors such as team size and goal type manifest in long running simulations. To overcome this gap, we conduct a controlled, full-factorial study examining how contextual factors affect collaboration behavior across multi-party simulation frameworks. Using well established social science taxonomies, we quantify context sensitivity of collaboration behavior in simulated teams. Our analyses reveal significant effects of contextual factors such as simulators consistently favor smooth collaboration over disagreement, negotiation pressure, and coordination breakdown. These findings provide the first systematic evidence of how contextual factors influence emergent collaboration in LLM based multi-party simulation frameworks, offering both guidance and empirical results for the use of such simulations.

title: Pano2BIM: A Geometry-Constrained Vision-Language Agent for As-Built BIM Generation from a Floor Plan and a Single 360$^\circ$ Image
authors: Juan Diego Casta\~no Molina, Borja Garc\'ia de Soto
abstract: Digital twins require accurate, up-to-date building information models (BIM) that reflect physical conditions, yet generating and maintaining as-built models remains costly and labor-intensive. Emerging image-based methods can capture visual appearance without inherently producing structured BIM information, while vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with reliable metric object placement. This paper presents Pano2BIM, a geometry-constrained VLM agent that generates approximate IFC4 models at Level of Development (LOD) 200 from a floor plan with known room dimensions and a single 360-degree photograph. The VLM identifies landmarks and objects, while deterministic tools estimate camera pose, compute metric positions through ray casting, and check spatial constraints. An optional second stage enriches the presentation model through render-and-compare feedback without modifying the primary furniture geometry. In a preliminary evaluation on one laboratory, the proposed Measure workflow achieved a mean furniture-footprint intersection over union (IoU) of 0.53, compared with 0.44 for a single-response baseline using identical modeling instructions, and matched an average of 4.0 versus 2.3 of seven fixed furniture elements across three runs. Centroid disagreements were similar for the four elements consistently identified by both approaches. The measurement stage averaged 3.8 minutes and USD 1.63 in API costs per run, while the complete demonstrated workflow required approximately 42 minutes and USD 11. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of rapid, low-cost as-built BIM generation, with potential applications in maintaining digital twins that reflect changing physical conditions.

title: A Novel Lightweight Multi-Scale Branching Encoder for Few-Shot Image Classification
authors: Oriod Malo (AI Lab UMT), Alexandre Xavier Falc\~ao (IC), Laurent Najman (KUSTAR, LIGM)
abstract: Few-Shot Learning (FSL) addresses classification scenarios in which only a small number of labeled examples are available for each class. This paper presents the Sum12 Multi-Scale branching encoder, a lightweight convolutional architecture designed to improve the embedding stage of Prototypical Networks without substantially increasing computational cost. The encoder uses seven parallel convolutional branches whose kernel-size combinations sum to 12, allowing local and broader spatial structures to be represented within a unified Multi-Scale feature space. The proposed architecture was evaluated on Omniglot, CIFAR- FS, FC100, and miniImageNet under controlled few-shot learning protocols and compared with the original Prototypical Network encoder and Inception-inspired branch variants. Additional ablation studies have investigated fusion strategies, dilated convolutions, branch compositions, and receptive field budget. Beyond few-shot learning, the encoder was also tested on the MedMNIST 2D benchmark to assess its behavior in conventional supervised medical image classification. Across these experiments, Sum12 generally improved the low-shot classification performance with respect to the basic ProtoNet encoder while preserving a compact model size. These properties suggest that the proposed encoder may be suitable for low-data visual recognition and resource-constrained intelligent imaging applications. However, complete end-to- end validation on the target embedded platform, including resolution of the observed implementation discrepancies, remains future work.

title: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video
authors: Junyan Huang, Sanskar Agmain, Chen Gong, Yan Pang, FNU Suya
abstract: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.

title: Dynamic Merging Mutually-Distilled Multi-View Networks for RGB-Event-based Representation Learning
authors: Futian Wang, Fan Zhang, Xiao Wang, Yuhe Ding, Shiao Wang, Jingxi Huang, Jin Tang
abstract: Multi-modal fusion algorithms combining conventional frame-based cameras and event cameras have recently attracted substantial research attention. Typically, existing approaches convert event streams into frames, voxels, or tensors, and then learn the required spatiotemporal information from these transformed event representations for fusion with conventional frame-camera data. Obviously, such paradigms only exploit the limited representational capacity of event data. Moreover, standard training pipelines fail to fully leverage diverse model parameters obtained throughout the learning process. In this paper, we propose a novel mutual distillation method leveraging multi-view teacher network weights to better integrate multiple event representations and achieve model-parameter level fusion. Specifically, we employ multiple encoders to extract different types of event representations and perform mutual knowledge distillation at both the feature-level and logit-level in this process. Afterwards, we perform a dynamic hierarchical model merge strategy on the model parameters from the first stage to yield a unified multi-modal RGB-Event representation model. Experimental results across multiple event-based datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves significant performance improvements.

title: Inverse modelling of a laser-plasma accelerator
authors: Mykyta Lenivenko (IJCLab), Arnaud Beck (LLR), Hayg Guler (IJCLab), Gueladio Kane (IJCLab), Sophie Kazamias (IJCLab), Viacheslav Kubytskyi (IJCLab), Bruno Lucas (IJCLab), Marceau Pintonato (IJCLab), Jana Serhal (IJCLab), Slava Smartsev (IJCLab), Kalyani Swain (IJCLab), Kevin Cassou (IJCLab)
abstract: The electron beams of a laser-plasma accelerator depend non-linearly on the laser and gas settings. This dependence is explored using particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations, and machine-learning models trained on these simulations predict the beam from the settings. Here we address the reverse problem: given a measured beam, which settings produced it? We infer three of them: the gas pressure $p\_1$, the normalised vector potential $a\_0$ and the nitrogen concentration $c\_{N\_2}$. The solution is not guaranteed to be unique. We train an ensemble of mixture density networks that, for each beam, output several possible sets of settings with their probabilities and uncertainties, and test them on simulated beams with realistic measurement noise. On average, the predictions are accurate ($R^2 = 0.91$), yet for about two-thirds of the beams the inferred distribution has two competing solutions. These share nearly the same value of $a\_0^2 p\_1$, which controls how strongly the laser focuses itself in the plasma and, in earlier PALLAS studies, when electrons start to be injected. Keeping this quantity fixed gives beams that are practically indistinguishable with realistic diagnostics. A forward model used as a check removes unphysical solutions but cannot choose between the two plausible ones. We then test two ways to resolve the ambiguity. Adding the full electron energy spectrum improves the mean prediction ($R^2 = 0.94$), mostly through $a\_0$. It changes the weights of the two solutions but does not move them. A second measurement at a deliberately different plasma density is more effective. In paired PIC simulations, it reduces the error on $a\_0$ by a factor of 2.6, whereas repeating the measurement at the same density brings almost no gain.

title: SpatialVec: A Unified Representation Learning Framework for Geospatial Objects with Boundary-Aware Sampling
authors: Samya Acharja, Kanchan Chowdhury
abstract: Spatial representation learning is essential for Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) applications, enabling machine learning models to capture the geometry, location, and spatial relationships of geographic entities such as points, polylines, and polygons. Existing spatial encoding methods often struggle to preserve fine-grained topological information, particularly for interactions involving complex geometries such as polylines and polygons. These approaches inadequately capture boundary structure and local spatial context, causing topology-sensitive relationships near geometry boundaries to be underrepresented in the learned embedding space. Consequently, accurately modeling complex spatial interactions remains a significant challenge for downstream spatial reasoning tasks. To fill the gap, we introduce SpatialVec, a boundary-aware spatial representation learning framework that adaptively samples geometry boundaries and their surrounding regions, capturing fine-grained geometric structures critical for topology-aware spatial reasoning. A transformer-based encoder-decoder trained through geometry reconstruction produces compact, geometry-aware, and unified representations for points, polylines, and polygons. Empirical evaluation on two real-world datasets shows that SpatialVec substantially improves the preservation of challenging topological relationships involving polygonal interactions and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines significantly on downstream prediction and classification tasks.

title: DTP-OPSD: Reinforcement Learning with Distractor-Aware Temporal-Privilege On-Policy Self-Distillation for Temporal Video Grounding
authors: Zhaoyu Chen, Yongwei Nie
abstract: Temporal Video Grounding (TVG) aims to localize the start and end times of an event described by a language query in a video. The task becomes particularly challenging when the same video contains multiple repeated, similar, or opposite events. On these hard examples, all responses sampled by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) may miss the target and receive zero temporal Intersection-over-Union (tIoU). Their group-relative advantages are then all zero, leaving no useful policy gradient signal. To address this, we propose DTP-OPSD, a reinforcement learning framework with distractor-aware temporal-privilege on-policy self-distillation. The student observes the clean video and generates responses on-policy, while a shared-weight teacher observes a privileged video in which the target window is marked by red full-frame borders and same-video distractor windows by blue full-frame borders. For the distillation loss, the teacher evaluates student-generated prefixes and provides dense token-level Jensen-Shannon divergence supervision. This supervision remains informative even when GRPO provides no policy gradient signal. We suppress distillation when the teacher does not outperform the student and strengthen it for groups where the teacher performs better but all student rollouts receive zero tIoU. We also construct a compact hard-interference training set through VLM screening and human verification. With only 300 additional post-training examples, DTP-OPSD achieves the highest mIoU among the compared open-source 8B models on Charades-TimeLens, ActivityNet-TimeLens, and QVHighlights-TimeLens, reaching 55.93, 54.77, and 66.71, respectively. Compared with Pure GRPO trained on the same data, DTP-OPSD improves all 12 reported metrics, with R1@0.7 gains of 1.28, 1.62, and 1.78 points on the three benchmarks. Code will be released at https://github.com/nian1125/DTP-OPSD

title: SPARQLcirc: Probabilistic Query Evaluation with Provenance Circuits
authors: Jingcheng Wu, Ratan Bahadur Thapa, Daniel Hern\'andez, Steffen Staab
abstract: Probabilistic query evaluation (PQE) computes the probability of every answer of a query over a tuple-independent probabilistic knowledge graph. We study exact PQE for SPARQL over graphs accessed through SPARQL 1.1 endpoints. Shared triples among the derivations of an answer make exact PQE #P-hard in general. Knowledge compilation of the Boolean provenance of every answer yields exact probabilities, and the provenance formulas of different answers can share subformulas. We propose SPARQLcirc, which rewrites a SPARQL query into CONSTRUCT queries that name every gate by its content, so that the results of independent queries form one Boolean provenance circuit for all answers. The rewriting covers joins, unions, projection, filters, OPTIONAL, difference, and transitive closures. SPARQLcirc compiles the circuit and computes the exact probability of every answer by weighted model counting. For the evaluation, we draw random probabilities for the triples of WatDiv and gMark and the statements of Wikidata and evaluate the CONSTRUCT queries on GraphDB, Fuseki, and Oxigraph. The ratio of the end-to-end time of PQE with SPARQLcirc to that of PQE by compiling the provenance expressions of the SPARQL provenance rewriting NPCS decreases with the number of derivations.

title: FB-MOAC: A Reinforcement Learning Algorithm for Forward-Backward Markov Decision Processes
authors: Mohsen Amidzadeh, Mario Di Francesco
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are effective in solving problems that can be modeled as Markov decision processes (MDPs). These algorithms primarily target forward MDPs whose dynamics evolve over time from an initial state. However, several important problems in different scenarios including stochastic control and network systems exhibit both a forward and a backward dynamics. As a consequence, they cannot be expressed as a standard MDP, thereby calling for a novel theory for RL in this context. Accordingly, this work introduces the concept of Forward-Backward Markov Decision Processes (FB-MDPs) for multi-objective problems, develops a novel theoretical framework to characterize their optimal solutions, and proposes a general forward-backward step-wise template that allows to adapt RL algorithms for FB-MDP problems. A Forward Backward Multi Objective Actor Critic (FB-MOAC) algorithm is introduced accordingly to obtain optimal policies with guaranteed convergence and a competitive rate with respect to standard approaches in RL. FB-MOAC is evaluated on diverse use cases in the context of mathematical finance and mobile resource management. The obtained results show that FB-MOAC outperforms the state of the art across different metrics, highlighting its ability to learn and maximize rewards.

title: Kerkoporta: Injecting Structured-Output Backdoors in Reasoning Coding Agents
authors: Georgios Syros, Blake Bullwinkel, Alina Oprea, Cristina Nita-Rotaru, Amanda Minnich, Xiaodong Liu, Giorgio Severi
abstract: Existing large language model (LLM) backdoor attacks operate primarily in chat settings, where the risk is bounded by free-form text outputs. AI agents remove that bound by performing actions and executing commands on the user's machine. We introduce structured-output backdoor attacks against reasoning models in agentic coding settings. A trigger placed anywhere in the agent's context causes the model to emit an attacker-chosen tool call, which the harness executes, directly compromising the system's confidentiality, integrity, or availability. We present Kerkoporta, a methodology that constructs high-quality poison samples, injects the backdoor via supervised fine-tuning, and recovers utility loss with lightweight reinforcement learning. We evaluate on modern, heavily post-trained open-weight models across proprietary and open-source harnesses, focusing on coding for its wide adoption and long-horizon task structure. The attack reaches success rates of up to 96.2% and can be configured to generalize across harnesses or bind to a single target. The resulting models can outperform the clean baseline on standard utility benchmarks, giving victims a direct incentive to adopt them. Overall, we demonstrate that LLM backdoors can have critical security impacts in the context of modern coding agents, and we characterize the poisoning methodology required to insert backdoors that are both effective and stealthy in this setting.

title: From Concepts to Actual Causes: Toward Closing the Concept-Malfunction Gap in Robot Foundation Models
authors: Gihyuk Ko
abstract: Post-incident analysis of a robot foundation model poses a singular causal question: which internal components caused this failure, and to what degree? Mechanistic interpretability (MI), however, establishes general causal claims by decoding the concepts a policy has learned, yet knowing which concepts are encoded is insufficient for identifying the actual cause of a specific incident. In this position paper, we analyze this concept-malfunction gap by posing fault isolation in the framework of actual causality. Specifically, we formalize a fault-isolation query as a tuple of intervened internal components, counterfactual values, contingencies, and read-outs, and lay out conditions for it to be well-specified. Through this lens, we identify shortcomings of current MI approaches: they assume fixed contingencies and read out only immediate effects, letting backups obscure actual causes. We demonstrate on a toy example that these shortcomings can lead to conflicting verdicts. Lastly, based on the well-specification conditions, we outline four open research tasks toward closing the gap.

title: FlowFPR: Flow Matching Prior for Oversampled Fourier Phase Retrieval
authors: Li Jiatai, Cao Wenfei, Chen Yang
abstract: Fourier phase retrieval reconstructs images from magnitude measurements without phase information, but noise and channel ambiguities make natural color-image recovery challenging. Although diffusion-prior methods provide strong image constraints, their recovery can deteriorate under stronger measurement noise, and repeated generative updates incur substantial computational cost. This paper proposes FlowFPR, which integrates a pretrained Flow Matching prior with relaxed averaged alternating reflections for oversampled Fourier phase retrieval. Each outer iteration obtains a clean image estimate through a single time-dependent Flow prediction, applies measurement-consistency correction, and reconstructs the next path state after fusing the two candidates. This process requires no backpropagation of measurement errors through the Flow network. To address ineffective or excessive correction caused by prescribed fusion weights and fixed inner depths, we introduce adaptive fusion based on residual improvement and a controlled inner search combining early stopping with best-so-far candidate selection. Their combination yields a joint variant alongside the basic method and the two independent improvements. Experiments on natural face images under a common ground-truth-assisted multiple-restart evaluation protocol show that the joint variant achieves the best mean quality among the evaluated methods at the two tested nonzero noise levels, while same-hardware timing demonstrates lower end-to-end runtime than the diffusion-based baselines.

title: A Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering Framework with Automated Cluster Cardinality Estimation Ability
authors: George Stamatelis, Konstantinos Koutroumbas
abstract: Fuzzy clustering provides a robust framework for handling ambiguous and overlapping data boundaries, yet its traditional formulation generates entirely dense membership assignments that limit noise resilience and prevent estimating the true number of clusters, when it is unknown. To address these limitations, we introduce in this paper the Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering (GSFC) framework, which incorporates a continuous sparsity penalty into the fuzzy objective function. Because closed-form solutions are precluded by the simultaneous presence of fuzzifier and sparsity exponents, we propose an efficient primal-dual bisection search coupled with specialized analytic pathways to rigorously enforce the partition constraint while organically driving trace memberships to exact zero. This mathematically enforced sparsity empowers the algorithm to autonomously estimate the true number of clusters by dynamically pruning redundant clusters, provided that it is initialized by a larger than the true number of clusters. Furthermore, we integrate a virtual noise sink to insulate outliers from the rest of the data points. The usage of the proposed framework is also extended to line segment detection. Extensive empirical evaluations across synthetic toy datasets, high-noise geometric stress tests, and real-world benchmarks (UCI wine dataset and hyperspectral images) demonstrate that GSFC effectively exceeds conventional fuzzy benchmarks while autonomously resolving cluster cardinality. Additionally, it significantly outperforms existing sparse possibilistic and probabilistic soft-clustering alternatives in line detection tasks.

title: Learning to bid and bundle: a posterior-sampling agent for online retail
authors: Hadi Mohammadi (Utrecht University)
abstract: An online retailer launching a perishable product bids for sponsored-search clicks, discounts a bundle with an always-stocked staple and displays its remaining stock, which raises willingness to pay. It knows neither how clicks respond to its bid nor how strong and dispersed its market is, and learns both over repeated seasons from data its own decisions censor: a zero bid reveals nothing about paid clicks, and choices follow only clicks. We design a posterior-sampling agent for it. Each period it draws a market from an exact posterior and posts the bid and discount of that market's exactly solved season plan, so every action is one a fully informed seller could take. In a simulated online florist it has the lowest regret averaged over markets. In weak markets it gives up 12% to 23% of one season's revenue over 500 seasons, four to seven times less than drawing once per season. A planner acting on point estimates can stop bidding and never learn that bidding pays. The agent escapes after about three seasons on average, against fifty with one draw per season. Where displayed scarcity keeps willingness to pay above the posted price, the discount needs no learning. Customers waiting for the discount to return to its recent level look like lost sales, so frequent waiting makes the agent underrate its market. One discount per season removes waiting at a cost of 5.9% of clairvoyant revenue in a weak market and none in a strong one.

title: Early Stopping in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey and Empirical Audit of Efficiency and Reliability
authors: Quang Hung Nguyen, Hanh Nguyen, Thanh Tam Nguyen, Quoc Viet Hung Nguyen, Trinh Pham, Thanh Trung Huynh
abstract: Large reasoning models can improve accuracy by generating longer reasoning traces, but some of this computation may be unnecessary. Early-stopping methods aim to stop once enough reasoning is available to answer. Evaluating these methods requires accounting for the cost of deciding when to stop and the reliability of the resulting answer. We evaluate different methods across five reasoning models on mathematical and scientific reasoning, code generation, and factuality tasks by using a shared rollout replay protocol. We introduce Target-Integrated Token Efficiency (TITE) to measure efficiency relative to the oracle across accuracy targets. We also examine correctness at later exit positions, transfer across models and tasks, post-stop reasoning continuation, and retained justification quality. In our experiments, correctness can decrease at later positions beyond what the fitted decoding-noise model predicts. Reliability checks also reveal continued reasoning after forced termination and weaker supporting reasoning in some correct early-stopping outputs. The implementation can be found in https://github.com/hung20gg/audit-early-stopping.

title: PatchScout: Thematic Web Data Collection via Information Foraging
authors: Michael West, Eduard Dragut
abstract: Researchers often need web corpora that are not answers to a single query, but reusable collections of documents spanning many decentralized sources. We refer to this problem as thematic web data collection: assembling semantically relevant documents that share a common theme but are scattered across heterogeneous and structurally disconnected regions of the web. Existing approaches, including traversal-based methods and LLM-driven web agents, are limited by local exploration or short-horizon stopping, preventing comprehensive collection. We formulate this task as a long-horizon information foraging problem over query-induced semantic patches, where the central challenge is deciding when to continue local exploitation and when to switch to new regions. We propose PatchScout, a multi-agent framework that instantiates a class of patch-switching policies to balance local exploitation and adaptive patch switching under a fixed budget. Experiments on four live-web topics show that PatchScout substantially improves yield and domain coverage over traversal-based and search-augmented reasoning agent baselines. In an applied social science setting with an incomplete prior collection, PatchScout discovers 102 previously unidentified entities, illustrating its ability to expand existing thematic datasets.

title: Reimagining Text-to-SQL: A Survey of Large Language Model Architectures and Strategies
authors: Shikhar Dave, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into executable SQL queries, democratizing access to relational data. Early approaches relied on handcrafted rules and template matching, while subsequent neural methods introduced encoder-decoder architectures, schema linking, and constrained decoding to handle increasingly complex queries. The emergence of large language models (LLMs), exemplified by systems such as ReFoRCE, Agentar-Scale-SQL, Snowflake's Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, and the modular XiYan-SQL framework, has dramatically advanced the field, pushing execution accuracy to new state-of-the-art levels on challenging benchmarks such as Spider, Spider 2.0, and BIRD. In parallel, modular frameworks decompose the task into sub-problems (schema retrieval, sketch-based generation, repair, and ranking), while agentic systems coordinate multiple specialized agents that communicate and dynamically allocate sub-tasks. This survey systematically reviews these LLM-driven approaches within a unified taxonomy of five paradigms (in-context learning, supervised and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, agentic and tool-augmented orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, and reinforcement learning) and characterizes them by model granularity (monolithic vs. modular), level of supervision (zero-shot, fine-tuned, or reinforcement-based), and reasoning style (direct decoding vs. decomposed multi-step reasoning). We further analyze evaluation metrics, datasets, and open challenges, including domain generalization, efficiency, and real-world deployment, and we examine the role of the semantic layer in production systems. As LLMs increasingly access sensitive databases, we also discuss responsible AI practices. We survey over 100 papers and technical resources, focusing on work published between 2022 and 2026.

title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
authors: Ziyin Zhang, Yuyu Guo, Ying Zhang, Siqiao Xue, Zihan Liao, Jin Qin, Wenjie Yang, Siyuan Yang, Shijie Li, Cheng Chen, Hao Wu, Zhaoyang Zhu, Ruipeng Li, Zhaokun Jiang, Lei Lei, Rui Wang, Hang Yu, Rui Wang
abstract: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

title: Interpretable structural temperature scaling for calibrating graph neural networks and point-cloud segmentation
authors: Chenyi Huang
abstract: Graph-aware calibrators make graph neural networks (GNNs) more trustworthy by predicting a temperature for each node, usually with auxiliary networks whose decisions are hard to inspect. We propose Interpretable Structural Temperature Scaling (ISTS), a twelve-parameter linear model that sets each node's temperature from named descriptors of its confidence, neighbourhood and closeness to labelled nodes, so every temperature traces back to descriptor contributions. ISTS preserves predictions, and cross-validated regularisation lets the calibration data decide how far the model departs from temperature scaling (TS). Its explanations are faithful at the level of node groups: on test nodes, ISTS softens groups that a global temperature leaves over-confident and sharpens under-confident ones (Spearman correlation 0.67 over 246 groups). On seven graphs with two backbones and eleven baselines, ISTS has the best average rank in negative log-likelihood (NLL) and Brier score and lowers NLL relative to TS by 1.8%, more than twice the gain of an identically fitted entropy-based temperature. It ranked first again on four held-out graphs under a protocol fixed in advance. From about 100 calibration nodes on, ISTS is a cheap and inspectable choice, and on point-cloud segmentation it significantly improves NLL, Brier score and the ranking of points for rejection.

title: AuroraWorld: Structured 4D World Modeling for Exo-to-Ego Video Generation in Robot Manipulation
authors: Hao Xue, Peng-Fei Zhang, Ying Cheng, Lanyun Zhu, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
abstract: Egocentric observations provide a robot-centric view of manipulation processes, capturing contact interactions and object-state changes that are important for visuomotor policy learning but difficult to observe from external cameras. However, collecting such data at scale remains expensive due to additional hardware requirements and platform-specific deployment costs. Synthesizing egocentric observations from large-scale exocentric manipulation videos provides a scalable alternative. However, existing methods struggle to synthesize physically consistent and policy-relevant egocentric videos under substantial viewpoint transformations, severe occlusions, complex object interactions, and inherently sparse observations from available exocentric viewpoints.

title: The Prior-Force Family of Implicit Denoiser Priors and Its Decisions in Linear Inverse Problems
authors: Weijie Liang, Chuling Wen, Jian Lu
abstract: Implicit priors given by Gaussian denoisers successfully regularize a wide range of inverse problems in approaches such as plug-and-play (PnP), regularization by denoising (RED) and score-based methods. Such a prior depends on the noise level, and how it selects among signals consistent with the data remains largely uncharacterized. To put implicit and explicit priors on the same footing, we define the prior-force family $W_t=t^{-1}(D_t^{-1}-I)$ of any Gaussian denoiser $D_t$ at noise variance $t>0$ (inverse in the graph sense), the normalized denoising residual as an operator on clean signals. At a common effective prior weight, the equilibrium equations differ only in their prior terms: PnP uses $W_t$, RED/score-based methods the score force (the normalized residual as an operator on noisy inputs), and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation the MAP force (the negative log-prior gradient). For the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) denoisers of a prior $\pi$, we compare the corresponding energies at three levels. Without observation, raising the noise level favors PnP minima that retain more posterior variance. On signals consistent with the data, the leading-order PnP energy for separated modes is the proximal hull of the MAP energy, which lets PnP select signals between modes; modes of equal data fit are ranked by peak height at small noise levels and by mass at large ones. For recovery, $W_t$ at the truth bounds the local bias, and an oracle noise level balances this bias against denoiser error. These results show that the noise level is a parameter of the prior rather than a step size. Experiments with exact priors support these predictions, including the mixture components that PnP selects on unseen data.

title: Neurons Are All You Need
authors: Joseph B. Alzagatiti, Alain C. Glanzman, Perry A. Demsko, Pablo I. Salanova, David L. Glanzman
abstract: For decades, artificial neural networks have operated under the assumption that durable, learned capability resides exclusively in adaptive synaptic parameters, primarily due to the established neurobiology of synaptic connectivity. This design forces models to remain stateless during deployment, incurring well-known limitations such as catastrophic forgetting and expensive retraining. However, recent neurobiological research by Glanzman and colleagues, and others, shows that memories can be transferred between individual organisms in a synaptically independent manner. Inspired by this research, we sought to demonstrate memory transfer of persistent memory between AI model instances, leveraging a neurocentric version of memory. In this paper, we propose NURESA (Neural Unit with Retentive Self-Adaptive Architecture), a novel neural layer that eschews sole reliance on synaptic weight updating by introducing persistent intra-unit memory as a first-class, computational primitive. By structurally separating computation from persistent memory, NURESA enables autonomous memory accumulation and consolidation into transferable stores of memory registers. Experiments across MLP, GPT-2, and modern frontier models like Qwen2.5 demonstrate qualitatively new capability: zero-shot transfer of learned capability into a naive model instance without retraining or access to the original training data; this transfer is enabled by a sparse set of parameters in NURESA's memory register that the model selects on its own based on which neurons were most active. The memory transfer capability of NURESA also protects against domain loss when transformer models undergo learning via fine-tuning. Finally, the memory transfer process completes in approximately one minute even for transformer models with millions to billions of parameters, producing a transfer file orders of magnitude smaller than the original model.

title: CAPER: Circuit-Aware Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in LLMs for Analog Verification
authors: Saion K. Roy
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate analog circuits, yet every netlist must also be verified. We propose LLMs as verification assistants for analog circuits that flag unmet specifications and reliability issues that appear under process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variation. These issues emerge from how circuit stages combine, a structure that generic parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA do not capture. To this end, we introduce CAPER, a circuit-aware PEFT method that adds a small branch alongside LoRA to read each stage's properties from the LLM and combine them from the relevant stages. In deciding whether a feedback loop is negative, LoRA and a high-rank adapter stay at chance, whereas CAPER answers every test case correctly. For comparator latches, where 11 of 90 LLM-written designs that work under nominal conditions fail under PVT variation, CAPER likewise learns to flag such latent failures, while generic adapters stay near chance. These results show that adding circuit knowledge to PEFT makes such analog verification checks learnable through fine-tuning.

title: MemU-Bench: Benchmarking GUI Agents on Long-Horizon User Interactions
authors: Yizhou Liu, Zhengxi Lu, Fei Tang, Yiwen Qiu, Yong Du, Tongbo Chen, Bofan Chen, Tao Jiang, Wenhao Xu, Yunfeng Shu, Wenqi Zhang, Weiming Lu, Jun Xiao, Yueting Zhuang, Yongliang Shen
abstract: Existing Graphical User Interface (GUI) benchmarks predominantly rely on precise and stateless user instructions. In everyday usage, however, instructions are often \emph{vague and history-dependent}: users omit the exact details of their past operations because they no longer remember them, leaving the agent to recover the missing context from long and noisy interaction histories. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce \textbf{MemU-Bench}, a mobile benchmark of \textbf{118 vague tasks} grounded in 29 long-horizon user trajectories, where agents must distill raw interaction streams into memory and retrieve the missing context on demand, with task outcomes verified against serialized application databases. Alongside Success Rate, we incorporate Interaction Efficiency (IE) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) to expose agents that succeed by exhaustively searching across different applications rather than by \emph{genuinely recalling} the history. Evaluations show that without user history, state-of-the-art systems struggle under such ambiguity: the best-performing Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves an SPL of only 16.4\%, and end-to-end GUI agents fall below 5\%. To address this, we further propose \textbf{AppMem}, a training-free framework that distills user history into a \emph{structured, app-centric} memory bank, tracks interrupted intents across application switches, and selectively retrieves relevant memories via target-app inference. AppMem raises the SPL of GPT-5.5 from 15.7\% to 66.9\% (\textbf{+51.2\%}), outperforms a naive summary baseline by 9.3\%, and delivers consistent gains across evaluated backbones.

title: OPINE: Orthogonal Projection in Invertible Nonlinear Embeddings for Turbulent Flows
authors: Anqiao Ouyang, Hongyi Ke, Qi Wang
abstract: Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) represents physical fields with orthogonal modes ordered by variance, so that one decomposition gives reduced coordinates in every dimension, but it needs many modes when the data lie near a curved manifold. Nonlinear autoencoders are more compact, but their information loss happens inside a nonlinear encoder, and a model trained with one latent dimension gives no model with a smaller one. We introduce Orthogonal Projection in Invertible Nonlinear Embeddings (OPINE), which learns an invertible nonlinear change of coordinates and performs POD in the transformed coordinates. Because the map is invertible, all information loss occurs in the POD projection, and ordering its basis after training gives reduced coordinates of every smaller dimension from a single model. Training alternates gradient updates of the map with a damped update that tracks the evolving POD subspace, and we prove that this update converges locally to the exact POD subspace. We evaluate OPINE on synthetic manifolds, chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamics, forced Burgers turbulence, two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow, and three-dimensional minimal channel flow. OPINE is more accurate than POD at every tested retained dimension above one, and on the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Burgers dynamics, it is more accurate than convolutional and fully connected autoencoders by more than two orders of magnitude at the largest retained dimension.

title: From Cross-Section to Cross-Omics: Conditional Cell Nucleus Image Editing in Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Yuechen Yang, Junchao Zhu, Junlin Guo, Yanfan Zhu, Ruining Deng, Zhengyi Lu, Tianyuan Yao, Chongyu Qu, Marilyn Lionts, Xingyi Guo, Yaohong Wang, Yu Wang, Shilin Zhao, Haichun Yang, Yuankai Huo
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) platforms simultaneously measure gene expression and capture cell nucleus images at single-cell resolution. A fundamental property of tissue preparation introduces a confounding relationship between the two measurement modalities: sectioning a three-dimensional tissue into a thin slice produces a two-dimensional cross-section whose area depends on the cutting angle. Larger cross-sections expose more cytoplasm, yielding higher mRNA counts, while pathomics features such as nuclear area are measured directly from the same 2D boundary. This sectioning geometry creates an apparent correlation between gene expression and pathomics that reflects the measurement process rather than independent biology. Existing gene-to-image methods generate cell images from gene features but do not support condition-driven editing of existing images across both omics layers. We apply the Manifold-Aware Diffusion (MAD) framework to this dual-omics editing setting, enabling targeted modification of one feature group while preserving the other. Evaluated on podocyte cells from CosMx SMI kidney tissue, MAD achieves MAE=0.6636 and FID=25.19 for pathomics editing, outperforming all compared baselines. A controlled simulation study further confirms that the VAE component in MAD better preserves cross-group independence than CCDM (MAD without VAE).

title: Spectral and Conformal: Neural Network Methods for Calibrated Trajectory Prediction and Control-Point Intervals
authors: Jasmine Ratchford, Raffaele Romagnoli
abstract: Autonomous systems that navigate their environment need methods to quickly assess the feasibility and safety of desired trajectories. Traditional solutions that rely on numerical integration can be computationally heavy, while fast data-driven surrogates lack the formal guarantees that numerical approaches provide. This work demonstrates a framework that uses (1) a neural network with a spectral backbone to learn trajectories and quantile bands with built-in constraints (initial conditions and stability); (2) a modified conformal quantile regression to provide calibrated, joint trajectory-level coverage; and (3) interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points. After refactoring the network for inference, the trajectory inference time for a quadrotor under a closed-loop linear quadratic regulator is 3.45~ms on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. The total pipeline time, including trajectory inference time, is 9.81~ms, or approximately 100~Hz, consistent with typical control rates.

title: Localized anomaly detection with a calorimeter normalizing flow
authors: Raunav Mendiratta, Jason Weitz, Javier Duarte
abstract: Normalizing flows trained as fast calorimeter simulators also give the likelihood of each shower, which can serve as an anomaly score. Because this likelihood sums over every voxel, a signal confined to a few voxels can be lost in the fluctuations of the rest of the shower. For example, in a public benchmark dataset in which a long-lived neutral particle decays to two photons, the CaloFlow likelihood used in previous work selects less than 5% of the signal at a background efficiency of $10^{-3}$ when the particle has the largest simulated mass and decays at or just behind the front face of the calorimeter. In this work, we define a regional anomaly score by summing the squared latent coordinates of the same flow within small detector regions around the point where the particle enters the calorimeter, with the threshold set using background showers alone. At the same background efficiency, this regional anomaly score selects more than 95% of the signal. The per-coordinate likelihood terms, summed over the same regions, perform equally well, but the squared latent coordinates have a known distribution for background showers and clearly illustrate when a shower departs from it. Therefore, normalizing flows may be sensitive to new physics, even if the global likelihood is not.

title: ProLand: A New Infeasible Manifold Optimization Method for LoRA Fine-Tuning
authors: Chenyu Zhou, Yuxuan Zeng, Qi Deng, Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye
abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model-rank configuration.

title: IsoAlign: Isoform-Aware DNA-Protein Alignment via Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
authors: Niousha Sadjadi, Arman Seyed-Ahmadi, Tony Tu, Micaela Elisa Consens, Kerr Ding, Alif Munim, Lila Kari, Zehui Li, Barry B. Rubin, Bo Wang, Vallijah Subasri
abstract: Genomic foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning DNA sequence representations, yet existing self-supervised pretraining strategies overlook alternative splicing and underperform compared to specialized models. To address this gap, we introduce IsoAlign, a multimodal framework that grounds genomic pretraining in isoform-aware DNA-protein alignment to learn biologically meaningful representations. IsoAlign aligns transcripts to their corresponding protein isoforms, capturing both coding sequences and broader regulatory contexts, using two Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA): DNA-Protein JEPA (DP-JEPA), which predicts protein representations from DNA using contrastive alignment, and Isoform-Masked JEPA (IM-JEPA), which models relationships among alternative isoforms of the same gene through masked protein prediction. We evaluate the learned DNA representations of these architectures across a multi-metric evaluation suite spanning tasks, including the prediction of pathogenicity, fitness, gene expression, and TF binding. Our results demonstrate that isoform-aware cross-modal alignment using JEPA significantly improves functional representations and downstream performance, establishing a promising direction for GFM pretraining.
