Ant provides complementary per-specification evidence, but its composite target has no positive violations and its any-violation target is single-class in most evaluated seed-condition slices. Overall, predictive robustness provides useful STL-specific ranking but little demonstrated additional ranking value over the current state; these findings caution against treating ensemble disagreement as a reliable indicator of safety uncertainty.

title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
authors: Ekaterina Seregina
abstract: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.

title: TIGER: Learning from Researcher Taste to Generate Tailored Research Ideas
authors: Shane Gu, Yufeng Lin, Dixi Yao, Xuchen Gong, Chenhao Tan
abstract: In pairwise comparisons where each judge chooses between an idea generated by its corresponding TIGER-8B policy and one generated by GPT-4.1, the three LLM researchers select the TIGER-8B idea in 56.6%-68.4% of 76 comparisons per researcher. PhD1 and PhD2 select the TIGER-8B idea in 19 of 30 pairs (63.3%) and 17 of 30 pairs (56.7%), respectively. All six directed cross-policy comparisons likewise favor the judge's matched TIGER-8B policy over an off-target policy, supporting the use of individual preference feedback for tailored research ideation.

title: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
authors: Shaohuai Liu, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du, Le Xie
abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.

title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction
authors: Faruk Alpay, Taylan Alpay
abstract: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\beta^{-1}\log T_\beta=1-\cos\phi$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.

title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
authors: Yaochen Wang, Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Haomin Zhuang, Xinyue Zeng, Han Chen, Kwesi Adu Cobbina, Dang Nguyen, Dianqi Li, Dawei Zhou, Tianyi Zhou
abstract: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

title: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models
authors: Sowjanya Karanam, Jayanth Bhargav
abstract: Machine learning systems are challenging to test using traditional software testing methods because their behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly programmed. This challenge is particularly significant in natural language processing (NLP), where small input variations can lead to unexpected model behavior. Conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, often fail to capture such inconsistencies. Metamorphic testing addresses this limitation by evaluating expected relationships between original and transformed inputs. With the increasing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and language-based AI systems, the need for systematic robustness testing has become even more pronounced. Motivated by this growing need, this paper presents a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach for evaluating the robustness of such systems. In particular, we consider sentiment analysis as a representative NLP task and evaluate a pretrained classifier under four transformations: synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation, and negation. Using consistency score, flip accuracy, and confidence change, we identify strengths in handling semantic variations and vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations. These findings highlight the value of metamorphic testing in identifying behavioral inconsistencies beyond conventional performance metrics and demonstrate its potential as a systematic framework for evaluating the robustness of language-based AI systems and guiding performance improvements before deployment.

title: Retrain, Alert, or Rollback? A Three-Response Decision Framework for Production ML Under Concept Drift
authors: Ali Sadeghian, Alireza Shafaei, Hamid Hadibeik, Babak Hossein Khalaj
abstract: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation. Every retrained model must pass a two-stage canary before promotion, and corruption-triggered and quality-triggered rollbacks enter different hold states. Under a prospectively specified protocol we compare RAR with six baselines, including a cost-aware retraining policy, on 13 streams: eight real public streams and five semi-synthetic streams derived from them. RAR does not dominate. At low retraining cost, retrain-heavy baselines lead, and no policy's rank differs significantly from RAR's. At higher cost, RAR beats detector-triggered retraining, periodic retraining, and no response simultaneously on four streams, each within a bounded cost window. Its advantage over detector-triggered retraining is consistent with a latency-feasibility condition stated in advance. Against the cost-aware policy, results are heterogeneous. RAR retrains before true drift onsets one eighth to one third as often as detector-triggered retraining, but at lower net utility on most semi-synthetic streams. On H2's designated corruption stream (a registered follow-up), rollbacks fire yet RAR loses to retraining baselines. At $\rho = 1$, removing the canary, and thus rollback, raises utility on 11 of 13 streams. On a post-hoc follow-up stream, cause-specific hold release resumes adaptation where a single cooldown does not. We provide the harness, configurations, and per-cell results for reproduction.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Evaluate Themselves? A Probabilistic VC Framework
authors: Jae Oh Woo, Mengdie Flora Wang, Rahul Ghosh, Baishali Chaudhury, Mun Young Kim
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) find increasing use in critical applications, evaluating their ability to assess their own outputs has become crucial. We present a theoretical and empirical framework that examines whether LLMs can differentiate between correct and incorrect solutions while maintaining properly calibrated confidence. Building on classical Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) theory, we adapt it to probabilistic predictors through two complexity metrics: Probabilistic VC (PVC), which measures a model's ability to confidently classify across problem types, and Calibration-aware PVC (C-PVC), which additionally demands alignment between confidence scores and actual success rates. Unlike Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Actual Error (AE), these measures give an integrated assessment of self-evaluation expressiveness and calibration, with sample complexity bounds and generalization guarantees comparable to classical VC theory. We test eleven 7-8B models on 360 original mathematical reasoning problems, TruthfulQA, and CommonsenseQA. Each model chooses between two of its own generated solutions and reports its confidence, with ground truth determined by an ensemble of larger models. The results show a systematic inverse relationship: models with greater self-evaluation expressiveness have weaker calibration. s1.1-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieve the highest PVC-VUS scores, while JiuZhang3.0-7B is best calibrated, with the lowest ECE and the smallest PVC-VUS gap. The trade-off persists across architectures, training paradigms, and domains, pointing to a fundamental challenge in developing self-reflective LLMs, and our framework offers practical tools for diagnosing it.

title: Partial Invariance for Classification under Structural Causal Models
authors: Austin Goddard, Yu Xiang
abstract: Making predictions in an unseen environment from data collected across multiple training environments is challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced when the target-generating mechanism varies across environments. In this work, we introduce environment-label separation, a form of partial environmental invariance that decomposes the target conditional distribution into an environment-invariant component and a label-invariant component. We show that this partial invariance enables estimation of the target conditional distribution in an unseen environment when using labeled training data together with unlabeled test features. Within the structural causal model framework, we provide sufficient conditions for environment-label separation. Building on these conditions, we develop an algorithm, dIMP-Classifier, which jointly minimizes an estimate of the test risk and encourages invariance across environments. We further provide finite-sample guarantees that characterize the test risk in terms of deviations from invariance, estimation error, and sample complexity. Experiments on simulated data and the real-world light tunnel Causal Chamber data demonstrate that the proposed approach can perform under interventions on the target mechanism and consistently outperforms the considered standard and invariance-based baselines.

title: Multiclass Classification with Rare Useful Features: Fundamental Limits and the Optimality of Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding
authors: Gabriel Moryoussef, Alon Kipnis
abstract: We consider classification in high-dimensional feature spaces where only a vanishing fraction of features are useful and the number of classes may be large. While this rare-and-weak useful-feature regime is well understood in the binary setting, its multiclass version raises new questions: a feature can be useful for class discrimination without separating any specific pair of classes. We focus on a rare feature diversity model, in which most features are useless, but a small fraction promote discrimination among classes in a way that can be detected by a per-feature diversity test, such as one-way ANOVA or the Kruskal-Wallis test. For this setting, we propose Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding (DP-HCT), a feature-screening procedure that applies a higher-criticism threshold to the collection of p-values obtained from per-feature diversity tests. We justify DP-HCT under a Gaussian multiclass Rare-and-Weak Useful Feature model with class-mean contrasts of fixed magnitude in random directions, extending the binary model of Donoho and Jin (2008). When the number of classes is fixed, our model recovers the binary phase transition. When the number of classes grows logarithmically with the number of features, however, we derive a new and strictly harder phase transition, driven by the growing degrees of freedom and their effect on the useful-feature tail rate. We show that whenever classification beyond chance is possible, DP-HCT with ANOVA, followed by a simple classifier based on similarity to class means, achieves asymptotically perfect accuracy. Experiments on real multiclass classification benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, and numerical simulations confirm that the derived phase-transition curve accurately predicts the finite-sample behavior of DP-HCT in the growing-class regime.

title: The 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model for Occupational Safety and Health
authors: Ramiro Pesina, Ashish Madkaikar
abstract: This paper presents the 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model, a progressive framework for Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) management that integrates Job Safety Analysis (JSA), dynamic risk assessment using leading and lagging indicators, and predictive analytics powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). The model provides organizations with a structured pathway to evolve from static, reactive safety practices to a sophisticated, predictive safety paradigm. Each tier builds upon the previous one, creating a comprehensive, data-driven approach that enables just-in-time training and preemptive risk mitigation.

title: Beyond Binary Detection: Type-Aware Hallucination Analysis and Hierarchical Detection in Financial Question Answering
authors: Xiongyu Chen, Sizhen Zhu, Zhuoer Wang
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions over financial filings, where an unfaithful answer can mislead investment, compliance, or client decisions. Hallucination detectors are a common safeguard, but they are usually evaluated with a single binary score that reveals neither which kinds of errors analysesed nor why. This paper studies hallucination detection on PHANTOM, a long-context benchmark built from SEC filings, at the level of hallucination type. We first analyze 15,443 paired hallucinated and faithful answers without any detector and find that hallucinated answers are more than twice as long as faithful ones, and that lexical grounding separates the two classes only because faithful answers are bimodal. We then generate hallucinations in nine financially motivated categories, confirm each with a separate verification pass, and diagnose an LLM-based detector on 4,086 usable examples. Generation success varies from 66.3% to 100% across categories. The detector reaches 80.2% binary accuracy but only 44.7% subtype accuracy, never assigns two of the nine categories, and misses between 5.3% and 46.8% of hallucinations depending on category; these misses are unrelated to input length but rise with how far an answer departs from the correct one. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose a two-stage hierarchical detector that first decides whether an answer is hallucinated and then assigns a subtype, raising binary accuracy to 95.6% and subtype accuracy to 56.1%. The results show that type-level evaluation exposes detector weaknesses that aggregate metrics conceal.

title: Overcoming Demand Censoring through Randomization for Risk-Sensitive Newsvendor Learning
authors: Zhengchao Wang, Nam Ho-Nguyen
abstract: We study online newsvendor learning with bounded demand, censored observations, and convex nonlinear shortage costs. Because stockouts can conceal the shortage magnitudes needed by gradient-based algorithms, we use randomized ordering to construct unbiased subgradient estimates. We characterize admissible randomization distributions within this framework and develop an online inventory policy that combines the resulting subgradient estimates with gradient-based updates. Our regret analysis quantifies the cost of randomization via the estimation variance and an additional loss term. We characterize the randomization distributions that minimize this objective. For piecewise-linear shortage costs, the optimal distribution is computed through a linear-time recursion; for costs with bounded curvature density, it is characterized by a scalar ordinary differential equation. The policy achieves expected regret of $O(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed order in hindsight over $T$ periods. Under independent demand and suitable curvature of expected losses, the bound improves to $O(\sqrt{T})$. Matching minimax lower bounds establish rate optimality over the corresponding classes with a fixed marginal-cost bound. Both rates extend to nonperishable inventory under uniformly positive conditional expected demand. Numerical experiments on synthetic and retail data show improvements over alternative policies using censored observations.

title: Qubrio: High-Performance Quantum Compilation via Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
authors: Jixuan Ruan, Zhuo Cui, Zhengding Hu, Zhongkai Yu, Xiang Fang, Yue Guan, Jason Ludmir, Phillip E. Weinberg, Xiuzhe Luo, Shengtao Wang, Sonia Lopez Alarcon, Hezi Zhang, Yufei Ding
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an adaptable alternative to traditional quantum compilation heuristics, which bottleneck progress by demanding costly manual redesigns whenever hardware evolves. However, naive single-pass LLM approaches fail under the unique challenges introduced by quantum compilation. We introduce Qubrio, a practical agentic framework that significantly reduces heuristic redesigns through a three-level decomposition. By (1) partitioning programs into sequential operation stages, (2) deploying specialized agents for placement, routing and optimization, and (3) using disaggregated feedback for precise error correction, our system reliably navigates complex physical constraints. Beyond serving as a direct compiler, our LLM framework also uncovers novel strategies that facilitate convoy-style shuttling, substantially enhancing hardware concurrency without sacrificing fidelity. We further integrate these strategies into the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) compiler, recovering a significant fraction of the LLM's performance advantages. On realistic workloads, our compiler achieves significant improvements in hardware runtime and program fidelity over the SOTA baseline PowerMove, seamlessly adapting to new hardware capabilities. Qubrio features an open user interface for practical use, and its code is publicly available at https://github.com/crosaa/Qubrio.

title: Hinted Scaling Laws
authors: Suze van Adrichem, Luke Bailey, Rohith Kuditipudi, Christine Ye, Neil Band, Ahmed Ahmed, John Duchi, Percy Liang, Tatsunori Hashimoto
abstract: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most $10^{20}$ FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a $10^{23}$ FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to $10^{22}$ FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

title: Current state of LLMs for Arabic dialectal machine translation
authors: Josef Jon, Rawan Bondok, Ond\v{r}ej Bojar
abstract: This work presents an evaluation of large language models (LLMs) for English to dialectal Arabic machine translation on the MADAR dataset. We evaluate both translation directions (English to Arabic and vice-versa) on 16 Arabic dialects. Our experiments cover a diverse set of models, including specialized Arabic models (Jais, Nile), multilingual models (Gemma, Command-R, Mistral, Aya), and commercial APIs (GPT-4.1). We employ multiple evaluation metrics: BLEU, CHRF, COMET (both reference-based and reference-less variants) and GEMBA (LLM-as-a-judge), as well as a small-scale manual evaluation, to assess translation quality. We discuss the challenges of automatic MT evaluation, especially in the context of Arabic dialects. We also evaluate the ability of LLMs to classify the dialect used in a text. The study offers insights into the capabilities and limitations of current LLMs for dialectal Arabic machine translation, particularly highlighting the difficulty of handling dialectal diversity, although the results may be influenced by possible training data contamination, which is always a concern with LLMs.

title: When the Text Is Silent: Memory Shortcuts and the Validity of LLM Annotation under Evidence Insufficiency
authors: Wenchang Wang, Yue Song
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate text for social science research, content moderation, and training data. Their broad knowledge of real-world entities raises a concern: when labeling a text, do they rely on its evidence or substitute what they already know? We call this behavior a memory shortcut and examine when it emerges, what amplifies it, and how to mitigate it. Using 995 widely recognized public figures and four matched control names per figure, we construct counterfactual texts that separate textual evidence from prior knowledge, and evaluate three commercial LLMs on 121,594 prompts each across five stages. We find a striking asymmetry. Although all models recognize nearly every figure, none follows memory over the text when the two conflict. Shortcuts instead emerge when evidence is absent: for one model, famous names raise the rate of remembered occupations, ages, and countries by 17.0, 14.9, and 6.8 percentage points relative to synthetic names. These effects occur only for recognized figures, and 98.6% of the resulting labels are factually correct about the namesake while none is supported by the text. Evaluation threats and answer-contingent rewards amplify shortcuts by 8.7 and 12.4 points. Famous names also raise leadership ratings of sparsely documented applicants by 0.22 and 0.28 points in two models. A namesake reminder and name masking each eliminate the shortcuts, with trade-offs in gender annotation. LLM annotations can thus be factually correct yet methodologically invalid. Trustworthy LLM annotation requires audits that test evidence absence, account for incentives in annotation instructions, and evaluate the attribute-specific trade-offs of mitigation.

title: Invertible Graph Aggregation Can Increase ReLU Readout Width
authors: Hiroyasu Usami, Masanori Tsukamoto, Kohei Hashiguchi
abstract: An invertible graph aggregation preserves the complete feature table, but can increase the size of a classifier that reads one node at a time. For every even $N\ge4$, we construct a labeled tree with $2N$ vertices and maximum degree three. A shared one-hidden-layer rectified linear unit (ReLU) classifier needs one hidden unit on the raw scalar features and exactly $N$ units after one lazy neighborhood mean. All aggregate values are distinct, and the mixing matrix has condition number at most 8. We determine the complete error curve for heads with a free affine term. The width separation persists under scalar perturbations. Under a specified bounded uniform-noise model with one nuisance coordinate, every one-unit aggregate head has expected error at least $1/12$, while a fixed $N$-unit head has zero error. Controlled fits compare trained heads with these explicit feasible scores. On Roman-empire and Tolokers, aggregation improves fitted prediction, and retaining raw features helps at the largest tested parameter budget. Training-only diagnostics include conditional output-layer optimality bounds for eight fixed runs.

title: Data-Scarce, Multi-Granular, Multimodal: Benchmark Design for Biosynthetic Gene Clusters
authors: Hanlin Xiao, Eriko Takano, Mauricio A. \'Alvarez, Rainer Breitling
abstract: Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are co-located genes that encode the biosynthesis of specialized metabolites, an important source of antibiotics, anticancer agents, immunosuppressants, and agricultural bioactives. Deep learning, particularly self-supervised foundation models, has spurred interest in BGC sequence modeling, but evaluation has lagged behind: existing benchmarks often rely on coarse classification over small curated datasets, providing limited discrimination among models and insight into downstream utility. We propose a benchmark-design framework in which an informative benchmark should be discriminative, separating models with statistical confidence, and applicable, spanning scientifically meaningful tasks under different levels of generalization. We instantiate this framework as BGC-Bench, which derives five tasks from MIBiG, ranging from A-domain substrate prediction to BGC-molecule retrieval, evaluates them under genotype- and phenotype-shift splits, includes an active-learning setting for label-scarce discovery, and is easily extensible to new tasks and encoders. BGCs further provide a shared testbed across granularities and modalities: BGC-Bench compares twelve encoders on nucleotide, amino-acid, or Pfam-domain sequences, including compositional baselines for each input type, and combines BGC and chemical encoders for cross-modal retrieval. No single representation dominates: the best granularity depends on the biological scale of the task, and pretrained encoders do not consistently outperform other representations across tasks and splits. Active-learning experiments show that most tasks remain data-limited, encoder rankings change with labeling budget, and acquisition strategies yield modest gains. These results show that BGC model evaluation requires task-diverse, shift-aware benchmarks, and the framework can be generalized to benchmark design beyond BGCs.

title: Atom-Wise Allocation of Message-Passing Scale for Molecular Property Prediction
authors: Regina Qianru Zhang, Honggang Wen, Zongru Li, Jinsong Ouyang, Zhiqin Chu, Pietro Li\`o, Xiaofeng Liu, Siu-Ming Yiu
abstract: Molecular properties depend on chemical structure at different ranges, from local polar groups governing solvation to extended substructures shaping bioactivity, yet graph neural networks usually fix one propagation scale for every atom. We present PRISM (Per-atom Routing over Intermediate States of Message Passing), in which each atom's encoded features produce a bounded scalar that positions a unimodal distribution over retained message-passing states and matching circular-fingerprint radii. Because one coordinate translates the whole profile, allocated depth responds to the routing scalar in closed form: at fixed temperature it is nondecreasing, its sensitivity scales with the profile variance, and it saturates in the clipped regions. Beyond providing closed-form analyzability, this constrained one-parameter profile matches or significantly outperforms parameter-matched, unconstrained node-wise gates and Jumping Knowledge attention. Under scaffold partitions with equal tuning budgets against eight graph, fingerprint, and geometric baselines, PRISM trained from scratch without three-dimensional coordinates achieves the lowest mean error on aqueous solubility and hydration free energy and strong accuracy on BACE and BBBP. As a general layer-combination rule, PRISM transfers directly to GCN, GIN, and GAT backbones, reducing hydration free energy error by up to 29% relative to last-layer readout. Applied to a pre-trained GIN, it improves on last-layer readout on four of six endpoints and gives the lowest lipophilicity error overall. In trained models, allocated depth differs systematically between atom types in a task-dependent way, and permuting profiles among a molecule's atoms raises prediction error on several endpoints, so the rule acts as a learned counterpart of atom typing.

title: Concise-9B: Removing the Slack from a Reasoning Model's Thinking
authors: Alexander Boesgaard Lorup
abstract: Reasoning models answer better when they think longer, but a thinking trace keeps going well after its answer has formed. We measure this slack in Qwen3.5-9B and remove most of it with concise self-training: two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning that keep the shortest correct samples, plus a small share of answer-synthesis targets, giving Concise-9B. On 8,983 held-out problems (competition and hard mathematics, SuperGPQA, a five-area confirmation set and MMLU-Pro), Concise-9B generates 0.66x the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B at a 32K thinking budget, with accuracy equivalent within +/-1 point (-0.20 [-0.77, +0.36] points). Forcing each trace on the hard and confirmation sets to answer every 2,048 thinking tokens, we find that 54-64% of Qwen3.5-9B's thinking tokens come after the point from which every forced answer equals the final one (41-48% for Concise-9B). Stopping there would keep every answer at 0.35-0.44x the base model's tokens, but finding that point takes hindsight: stopping when three consecutive forced answers agree costs the base model 2.4-9.2 points. Concise self-training removes slack without that cost: 86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens it saves come after the answer has formed. It has a limit: with traces continued to 80K tokens, Concise-9B solves 25 fewer of 1,276 hard problems (-25 [-49, -1]), mostly in competition mathematics. The measurement also yields a cheap commit signal for adaptive sampling that matched two-sample escalation within +/-1 point at 0.67x its tokens in a pre-registered test. Results on Qwen3.5-4B, on which the recipe was developed, and a replication on Olmo-3-7B-Think suggest that the saving depends on how verbose the base model is.

title: Toward Agentic AI-Ready Workflows in Built Environment Organizations: Knowledge Structures and Interoperability Challenges
authors: Ahmet Bahaddin Ersoz, Justin McHenry, Yevgeniya Kovalchuk, Edward Barrett, Mandana Sarey Khanie
abstract: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, and asset registers, with unstructured ones, including technical reports, design narratives, planning and policy documents, contracts, meeting minutes, and risk registers. This paper reviews how built environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability, and access and integration mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Drawing on existing literature, it examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data and considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents in a reliable manner. The paper synthesizes current perspectives, highlights challenges around fragmentation and interoperability, and identifies open questions for future research on AI-compatible information management in the built environment.

title: FactorSpec: Serving Exact Relational Constraints as Speculative Drafts
authors: Jianchang Su, Dawei Xiang, Wei Zhang
abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM serving by drafting tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, and its gain grows with the drafts the target accepts. Structured outputs should be an ideal case, because much of a record follows from relations among its fields: an itinerary's days follow from its cities' stays and flights. Serving engines, however, draft such text by proposing it from the prompt or a learned head, and their grammar masks enforce only syntax, so the model must satisfy the relations, which it violates: on NATURAL PLAN's trip problems, Qwen3-8B writes a valid itinerary for 10%, and retries that name the violated relation raise this to 14%. We present FactorSpec, which serves exact relational constraints as speculative drafts. FactorSpec compiles a JSON Schema and its relations into a factor graph with an exact feasibility check, drafts every token the constraint determines as certain, verifies each request at a width chosen for it, and computes the masks in worker processes outside the scheduler while the GPU runs. In SGLang, its drafts yield up to 10.5 tokens per verify step, up to 1.9x those of the fastest n-gram drafter, and it decodes up to 1.43x faster than speculators tuned per load, at a grammar mask's cost; it also leads in vLLM. Because every record is also valid, it serves up to 13.9x the valid records per GPU-second of syntax-only baselines.

title: Lie Routing Vision Language Models for View-Robust 3D Understanding
authors: Jingjun Yi, Chen Hu, Qi Bi, Hao Zheng, Huimin Huang,  Yongkang, Wei Ji, Yawen Huang, Xian Wu, Yefeng Zheng
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in 3D scene understanding from multi-view RGB observations. Yet a fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon we characterize as viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We introduce LieVLM, a Lie routing framework for view-robust 3D understanding. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, Lie routing adapts visual representations by applying local $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens extracted by VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients. A closed-form Pad\'e--Cayley map transforms projected visual features, whose identity-relative corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features. This design retains the pretrained semantic and direct spatial context while learning view-dependent feature adjustments. Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine the roles of geometric conditioning and transformation structure. Viewpoint analyses further reveal systematic variation in the predicted routing states alongside more localized target responses and stronger task performance across viewpoint changes.

title: CytoWave: Perturbation-Centric Pretraining for Single-Cell Response Prediction
authors: Yuwei Miao, Jingquan Yan, Hehuan Ma, Thao M. Dang, Lin Xu, Siyuan Zhang, Junzhou Huang
abstract: Predicting gene expression under perturbations from single-cell data is a fundamental task for modeling cellular responses, with applications in discovering gene function and designing therapeutics. However, existing methods often struggle to generalize across datasets due to differences in experimental protocols, biological contexts, and species. We present \textbf{CytoWave}, a perturbation-centric pretraining framework for single-cell genetic perturbation response prediction. We leverage large-scale cross-species perturbation datasets unified via orthology and train CytoWave in a two-stage manner. In the first stage, we learn reference control cell states via masked gene expression recovery on unperturbed cells. In the second stage, we pretrain the model to predict perturbed gene expression given control states and perturbation signals, together with a contrastive objective that aligns latent representations of perturbation responses with perturbation signals. We perform strict dataset-held-out evaluation across multiple condition combinations and case studies of pathway activity changes, demonstrating consistent and effective performance of CytoWave in predicting single-cell genetic perturbation responses.

title: Improving Financial Cybersecurity Through Fraud Transaction Detection with Deep Learning
authors: Harish Kant Pathak, Rahul Kumar
abstract: Financial fraud detection remains a critical challenge in cybersecurity, with traditional rule-based systems struggling to keep pace with evolving attack patterns. This paper presents a deep learning approach for fraud transaction detection, leveraging neural network architectures to identify anomalous financial behaviors with high accuracy. We evaluate multiple deep learning models including LSTM, CNN, and hybrid architectures on real-world financial transaction datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over conventional machine learning baselines. Our approach achieves robust performance in detecting fraudulent transactions while minimizing false positives, providing a scalable solution for enterprise financial cybersecurity systems

title: GRIPS: An Empirical Study of Pre-SQL Grounding Information for SQL Generation
authors: Ekata Mitra, Yufei Tao, Kamalamalini Nagasundaram, Ameeta Agrawal
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems answer natural language questions over structured data, but can fail before SQL generation by linking question mentions to the wrong table, column, value, or relation. Even valid SQL can then return an incorrect answer. This raises a central question: What pre-SQL information helps a SQL generator, and when does additional information cease to help? We investigate this question on TempTabQA-C and BIRD. Among the audited SQL Static failures, grounding errors form the largest category on both benchmarks. We introduce GRIPS (Grounding Representation and Input Processing for SQL generation), a three-stage method that derives structured pre-SQL information to make these decisions explicit before query generation. Across GPT-5-nano and Llama-70B, GRIPS-Adaptive improves over SQL Static in 18 of 20 settings, with an average accuracy gain of 11.8 percentage points, while reducing model-call token usage by 47.8%. Our controlled analysis shows which grounding information can improve SQL generation, whereas adding more pre-SQL information does not consistently help. By separating question-input grounding from SQL generation, GRIPS makes text-to-SQL more accurate, efficient, and easier to diagnose.

title: A Capitulation Direction Emerges With Scale and Is Causally Load-Bearing Where Validation Is Strong: Eight Models, Two Families, and Five Measurement Hazards
authors: Saad Aamir, Muhammad Awais Bin Adil
abstract: Sycophancy in language models is well documented as a behaviour but poorly localised as a mechanism. We ask whether capitulation under user pushback, the abandonment of a correct answer when a user objects, corresponds to a linear direction in the residual stream, and whether such a direction emerges with scale. Across eight instruction-tuned models spanning 0.5B to 14B parameters in two families, under a pre-registered protocol with leave-one-question-out cross-validation, within-question permutation nulls, and a positive control, we find no usable direction below 7B and a direction that clears our validation gate at 7B, 8B and 14B. Ablating that direction in Qwen2.5-7B reduces the rate at which the model reverses a correct answer by 4.8 percentage points, roughly a quarter in relative terms, while the identical intervention on a gate-failing direction and on a marginally passing one produces no effect. Probe quality, not statistical significance, predicts causal relevance. Behaviourally, pushback destroys three to five times more correct answers than it repairs at 1B and reaches parity by 7B, falsifying our own pre-registered prediction, and a sign-reversing crossover between pushback types survives an order of magnitude of scale in Qwen and holds at 8B in Llama, with marginalisation over five paraphrases per type. We additionally quantify five measurement hazards, including a numerical-precision effect that changes roughly one episode label in ten.

title: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents
authors: Jae Wang Lee, Abhirup Banerjee, Yeong Chan Lee
abstract: Medical artificial intelligence agents should retrieve patient identifiers only when a task requires them, the data-minimization principle behind the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for protected health information (PHI). An agent can retrieve identifiers without revealing them. Such silent access remains invisible to evaluations that inspect only the output. We embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked each tool invocation to canary exposure in the final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks. Three models invoked the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 did not. Stronger boundaries reduced this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy was confined to frames in which the user overrode the policy or asserted approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminated this access. Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access; boundaries, gates, and access-log audits are required together.

title: Coalitions, Stability, and Majority Jackpots: Frameworks for Unifying Majoritarian and Proportional Allocation in Multiwinner Elections
authors: Kit Scriven, Nitin Kohli
abstract: Social choice literature on multiwinner elections tends to focus on characterizing two distinct tasks: majoritarian representation and proportional representation. However, many real world systems can be viewed as operating between these two extremes, such as majority jackpot systems used in several countries throughout history. Towards the goal of better understanding these systems from a social choice perspective, we introduce two frameworks that encompass existing desiderata for majoritarian and proportional settings: coalitions, which encompasses properties such as fixed majority and solid coalitions; and stability, which encompasses various generalizations of Condorcet's criterion for single-winner elections, such as Gehrlein stability and local stability, among others. We develop theory and tools that characterize the mathematical and computational aspects of both frameworks across a wide array of preference structures (such as the unrestricted domain over candidates and the restricted domain of party lists). Building on this foundation, we shed new light on majority jackpot electoral systems, which to date have received limited mathematical analysis in the social choice literature.

title: Spatial Transfusion: From Structured Spatial Scene Understanding to Generation and Editing
authors: Jaeyeon Kim, Sebastian Braun, Hannes Gamper
abstract: Spatial audio conveys not only what sounds are present, but where they originate and how they interact with the environment. Recent audio-language models increasingly understand and reason about such scenes, yet spatial audio understanding, generation, and editing remain largely separate. We present Spatial Transfusion, a unified first-order ambisonics (FOA) framework that extends a pretrained spatial audio understanding model to generation and editing through flow matching over VAE latents. We formulate editing as a structured scene transformation over a taxonomy of atomic edits. Keeping the pretrained backbone frozen, we introduce modality-based LoRA routing and a curriculum that progressively adds generation, editing, and natural-language interaction. Experiments show that Spatial Transfusion largely preserves spatial understanding while outperforming full fine-tuning in generation and editing. The resulting model supports controllable FOA generation and editing through both structured and natural-language interfaces. Audio samples are available at https://microsoft.github.io/spatial-transfusion/

title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
authors: Sreehari Sankar, Debargha Ganguly, Vikash Singh, Mohsen Hariri, Weicong Chen, Yanyan Zhang, Shouren Wang, Wang Yang, Chaoda Song, Alexander Nemecek, Osama Zafar, Idan Davidovich, Yuting Shao, Kai Ye, Biyao Zhang, Xinpeng Li, Joe Stubbs, Erman Ayday, Jing Ma, Vipin Chaudhary
abstract: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.

title: When Does Adaptive Halting Win? Selection Rules Matter in Looped Language Models
authors: Mahesh Reddy Pagadala
abstract: Looped language models can stop iterating early, and recent work shows that post-hoc readouts of the loop trajectory often rival the learned exit gate of the looped model Ouro. Such comparisons reduce each method to one operating point chosen by a selection rule. We ask whether that rule decides the outcome. On a frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, we compared a trained stability probe ($\pi_1$-x) with Ouro's native gate, adapted to a per-question stopping decision, in pre-registered studies; the confirmatory study was designed after an exploratory finding on development data and evaluated once on a sealed test set of 8,517 questions. In the pre-registered confirmatory comparison, which selected operating points with a bootstrap-screened 1 pp accuracy-loss rule, the probe saved more of the four-loop budget than the native gate (+0.053 gross macro saving over three benchmarks, 95% CI [+0.049, +0.057]), mostly from CommonsenseQA, where the probe's test upper bound on accuracy loss exceeded 1 pp. Under a point-only rule, a pre-specified secondary analysis on the same test set reversed the preference (-0.022 [-0.026, -0.018]), with operating points that exceeded the budget. In pre-specified secondary comparisons, the probe showed no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL divergence between successive loops (+0.00125 [-0.0041, +0.0065]); we emphasise this result post hoc and claim no equivalence. The probe also broke its budget on one of two out-of-distribution benchmarks (3.26 pp loss on Social IQa). Savings are estimated from stored full-depth traces, not measured inference time, and our screen carries no formal risk-control guarantee. We conclude that halting methods should be compared as signals together with selection procedures, with strong untrained baselines and out-of-distribution checks.

title: Does a Norwegian further-trained model give more outdated legal values than its base model? A preregistered paired comparison of Borealis 2 and Gemma 4
authors: Eirik Botten Nicolaysen
abstract: We compare how often two released language models give outdated numeric values from Norwegian statutes and regulations: NbAiLab/borealis2-26b-a4b-preview (Borealis 2), which the National Library of Norway further trained from google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (Gemma 4), and Gemma 4 itself. The study was preregistered (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23858965) and uses the closed norregel benchmark, scored deterministically against a value history. On the 411 of 503 primary items where both models gave an interpretable answer, Borealis 2 alone was outdated on 10 items and Gemma 4 alone on 11 (d = -0.2 percentage points, 95% cluster bootstrap interval [-2.7, +2.5], exact one-sided McNemar p = 0.668). By the preregistered rule this is no effect of interest: the whole interval lies within the smallest effect of interest of +/-10 percentage points. Among the secondary measures, only the share of answers giving a value that took effect after the question date differs after Holm correction; Gemma 4 gave such answers more often. An exploratory comparison of two smaller Borealis models had no discordant pairs and is not informative. The design compares released models and does not isolate the effect of any part of their training.

title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
authors: Farnoush Rezaei Jafari (Technical University of Berlin, BIFOLD - Berlin Institute for the Foundations of Learning and Data), Tristan Lazard (Microsoft Research), Kenza Bouzid (Microsoft Research), Shruthi Bannur (Microsoft Research), Jeremiah Wander (Microsoft Research), Ashley Mae Conard (Microsoft Research), Stephanie Hyland (Microsoft Research), Lorin Crawford (Microsoft Research), Daniel Coelho de Castro (Microsoft Research)
abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

title: Embedding a de Rham Complex Structure into Eig-PIELM for Maxwell Eigenvalue Problems
authors: Hao Kang, Liang Li, Xing Li
abstract: The perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary condition alone does not eliminate the gradient nullspace of the Maxwell curl-curl operator. Consequently, a boundary-only Maxwell implementation of Eig-PIELM, an eigenvalue extension of the physics-informed extreme learning machine (PIELM), may retain represented gradient modes in its reduced trial space, producing nonphysical, gradient-contaminated modes. We develop dR-Eig-PIELM, a finite-dimensional structure-preserving extension that retains the linear-coefficient, boundary-null-space, and one-shot multimode architecture of Eig-PIELM. It combines compatible tensor-product grad--curl trial spaces with a constrained null-space construction to restrict the sampled PEC space to the mass-orthogonal complement of the represented gradient image before the eigensolve. Symmetric weak-form Gram assembly yields a symmetric-definite reduced eigenproblem without an eigenvalue cutoff under the stated sampling and material-positivity assumptions. For rectangles and cuboids, we establish fixed-degree exactness at the PEC vector-field space and derive rank and dimension identities. Numerical experiments show that dR-Eig-PIELM excludes the spurious eigenmodes with significant gradient components observed in the boundary-only baseline. The method exhibits rapid convergence with increasing polynomial degree and competitive work--precision performance in the tested configurations. A covariantly mapped waveguide example illustrates the potential of dR-Eig-PIELM for integration into design optimization workflows through a constrained local geometry update driven by computed cutoff frequencies and their sensitivities. This work provides a mathematical and computational framework for separating represented gradient modes from physical Maxwell eigenmodes within Eig-PIELM and supports its use in waveguide spectral analysis and geometry design.

title: MemShift: Separating Detection from Repair in LLM-Derived Personal Memory
authors: Zichuan Xu, Haochen Zhang, Yuyang Dong, Makoto Onizuka, Chuan Xiao
abstract: AI assistants store values that a language model derived from a person's records under the person's own definitions, such as their important contacts. Keeping such a value correct takes two steps: detection, noticing that an input changed, and repair, producing the correct new value. Benchmarks that score only the final answer cannot tell which step failed, and they state every change as new text. Seeing this limitation, we present MemShift, a benchmark of five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. The first three fork a synthetic world into branches that differ only in the shift. Gold values and dependencies are fixed before any text, and a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge. For a memory that reports its invalidations, MemShift shows for each changed item whether the memory noticed the change and whether its repair was right. Moreover, we build a reference memory with known detection and repair to validate the measure. By evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that detection helps only as much as repair allows: the LLMs re-derive few values computed by the person's definitions correctly, and programs that the LLM writes over typed records close most of the gap to exact recomputation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zichuanxu/memshift.

title: On Stochastic Continuous-Time Linear System Identification for Adaptive Stabilization
authors: Reza Sadeghi Hafshejani, Mohamad Kazem Shirani Faradonbeh
abstract: Learning to stabilize an unknown continuous-time stochastic linear system is a central problem in control theory and reinforcement learning. This paper numerically studies data-driven identification of such systems with possibly unstable dynamics for the purpose of stabilization. We present a method that learns a stabilizing gain from observed trajectories, and examine how the failure probability, namely the probability that the learned gain does not stabilize the system, depends on the amount of data, dimension, noise intensity, excitation, and controllability. Numerical experiments on an unstable batch-reactor benchmark show that the squared identification error decays inversely with the aggregate observation time, that is, the combined length of all trajectories, while the failure probability decays exponentially in the same quantity. Hence, despite instability, a single long trajectory can achieve similar stabilization performance to that of many short trajectories of the same total length. We also observe \emph{signal saturation}: stronger excitation improves stabilization only logarithmically with the excitation strength. Finally, we show experimentally that accurate identification of the full dynamics is \emph{not} necessary for successful stabilization.

title: AgiWorld: An Agentic Video World Model for Building Persistent Worlds
authors: Shaoheng Fang, Yiqun Mei, Hanwen Jiang, Xin Sun, Haitian Zheng, Hao Tan, Kalyan Sunkavalli, Georgios Pavlakos, Qixing Huang, Yiwei Hu
abstract: Recent interactive video world models generate visually compelling videos from a single image, following user-provided camera motion and text prompts. However, such low-level control demands substantial user effort to realize a high-level intent, and the generated world struggles to remain persistent as the exploration proceeds. In this work, we present AgiWorld, an agentic video world model that explores and builds a persistent world from a single image and a free-form instruction. For high-level planning, our agent AgiWorld-Agent designs the world and the journey through it in a world state and directs the exploration. For low-level realization, our video world model AgiWorld-WM generates the video chunk by chunk and stores it with its geometry in a spatial memory, from which the agent updates its world state. This closed loop keeps the world faithful to the user's intent and keeps the agent's world state consistent with the generated content throughout the exploration. We co-design the two levels around the shared spatial memory and an interface of metric camera trajectories and structured prompts. In AgiWorld-WM, to handle occlusion and accumulated geometric errors in the spatial memory over long rollouts, we propose occlusion-aware history selection, which retrieves past views by surface visibility, and reliability-based memory maintenance, which prefers reliable geometry and earlier observations. AgiWorld-WM achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks, and qualitative results and ablations show that AgiWorld builds persistent worlds from free-form instructions over minute-long journeys. Persistence thus arises not from the video model alone but from its closed loop with the agent.

title: Which Words a Model Fears: From a Refusal Direction to a Vocabulary-Wide Fear Lexicon
authors: Boyuan Zhang, Mohammad Zandsalimy, Shanu Sushmita
abstract: Whether an aligned language model refuses depends in part on which words a prompt contains, regardless of whether those words carry the request's meaning. Harm words shift the hidden state at the generation boundary along a component shared across prompts and words, which crossed differencing extracts as a single direction. In eight models, writing along this direction raises and lowers refusal monotonically with dose, ahead of random and KL-matched directions. Used as a ruler over the full vocabulary, the direction gives every word a shift, from "feared" words at one end to "courage" words at the other; a word's shift is predictable from its own representation, and appending a feared word to a benign prompt is enough to make the model refuse it. Two held-out tests validate the ranking in all eight models: refusal after inserting an unseen word rises with its table shift, and replacing a prompt's most feared word by its most courageous meaning-preserving synonym significantly raises the answer rate on benign and harmful prompts alike, by an amount that follows the shift the replacement actually causes.

title: VisCodeBench: a new benchmark dataset for Text-to-Vis reflecting real-world practice
authors: Hy Nguyen, Thomas James Elton, Ella Wilson, Andrew Reeson, Cecile Paris, Josiah Poon, Jonathan K. Kummerfeld
abstract: Generating visualisations from natural language requests (text-to-vis) enables users to explore data more efficiently. While LLMs can complete simple visualisation requests, their performance on challenging ones is not well covered by existing benchmarks. We introduce VisCodeBench, an end-to-end text-to-vis benchmark with 2,672 samples from three different domains: educational, scientific, and general audience scenarios with varying levels of complexity. We benchmark three visualisation systems---Codex, Claude Code, and LIDA---paired with a range of open and commercial LLMs across seven metrics covering execution, chart content, and visual quality. While basic execution is near-solved for strong systems, no system comes close to reproducing the reference data, with the best displayed data similarity reaching only $0.81$ and falling to $0.69$ on our hardest subset for this metric. We further find that frontier models separate on chart correctness and efficiency, with ClaudeCode-Opus-4.7 improving chart correctness by around 5 points over Codex-GPT-5 while running roughly 20 seconds faster. Separately, we find that system design matters as much as the underlying model: despite both running on GPT-5, Codex clearly outperforms LIDA, showing that the surrounding prompting, execution, and refinement pipeline can shape outcomes as much as the model itself. Finally, latency remains a practical obstacle, as even the strongest systems take 39-78 seconds to produce results. VisCodeBench is available at \href{https://github.com/SAIPLL/VisCodeBench}{https://github.com/SAIPLL/VisCodeBench} and accessed via a leaderboard; the full dataset is kept private to prevent LLM training use.

title: Exploiting Textual Semantics for Robust Cross-View Object Correspondence
authors: Bing Fan, Yunhe Feng, Yan Huang, Heng Fan
abstract: Cross-view object correspondence (CVOC) aims to establish associations of the same target between query and search videos captured from different viewpoints. Existing methods often rely on visual cues for CVOC. Despite recent progress, these methods struggle in complicated scenarios with substantial viewpoint changes and appearance variations, due to lacking sufficient target information. Addressing this, we introduce TeSCo, a framework that exploits rich Textual Semantics of an object, in addition to its visual cues, for cross-view object Correspondence. Our key insight is, textual description of a target, by capturing diverse attributes such as category, texture, and color, provides viewpoint- and appearance-invariant semantics, which are complementary to visual cues and can hence enhance correspondence robustness in complicated scenes. Inspired by this, TeSCo first generates a textual expression of the target from the given query view using a vision-language model, and then extracts textual feature to enhance visual features for localization in the search view. To realize this, we introduce a text-conditioned cross-modal fusion (TCF) module that incorporates the textual feature into visual features with text-guided modulation, producing more robust multimodal target representation for object correspondence. Since not all textual cues are equally compatible with the target in current search-view frame, we propose an iterative textual feature refinement (ITFR) module that progressively adjusts textual feature using search-view information before the TCF module, enabling search-view-aware textual semantics to be fused into visual features and leading to better performance. In extensive experiments on Ego-Exo4D and HANDAL-X, TeSCo demonstrates state-of-the-art results and largely outperforms other models, validating its efficacy. Our code is released at https://github.com/VAIL-Fan/TeSCo.

title: Agent Memory as Rate-Limited Filtering: Explicit State Outlasts Long Context Beyond a Reader-Dependent Horizon
authors: Tianhao Guo, Chongyao Guo
abstract: Can a language model that reads the full history of an access log say whether a service may act now? On an executable benchmark of grants, withdrawals, reinstatements, expiries, groups and change windows under a known policy, scored on pairs of histories that differ only in the order or one field of the deciding events, open models of 7 to 32 billion parameters fall from 72 to 86 percent after eight or sixteen events to 48 to 55 percent after 256, while reasoning-trained 32B models reading the current state reach 96 and 98 percent. A reasoning model of 120 billion parameters trails the state by four and seven points at 256 and 512 events and by about ten at 1,024, so the length beyond which explicit state outlasts long context grows with the reader. We treat agent memory as recursive filtering. The decision depends on the history only through a state whose size is set by the number of tracked keys. A store holding fewer component records than the state forgets on a time scale set by its capacity, and a reader model predicts its accuracy within 0.02 on average in a registered test. Retaining log lines without regard to time order errs with probability approaching one half, a bound that is attained. A filter in which a model parses each line and an explicit rule applies the updates answers 80 to 89 percent at 256 events and beats relevance retrieval, model-kept ledgers, a reimplementation of StateMem and the Mem0 library. A retriever that selects at query time the lines the queried state depends on matches it at 256 events on the first domain, so what decides is selection by the state's dependencies, which the filter performs when writing, without the query. Applying parsed updates themselves, the models fall to 58 and 59 percent. A frozen replication on a second domain with fresh wording reproduces the horizon.

title: Prior Action Control Causally Alters Language-Model Plasticity
authors: Marc-Andre Schulz
abstract: Two copies of one language model start from identical weights and receive the same rewards during training. For one copy the rewards depend on its own answers. The other copy is yoked: it receives the first copy's rewards no matter what it answers, a design taken from the learned-helplessness experiments of animal learning. We ask whether the copy whose rewards depended on its answers, the copy with control, later learns a new task faster, that is, whether control changes the model's plasticity. In Experiment 1, copies of Qwen3-0.6B generated their own answers in a two-turn game and afterwards learned a new task. The copies with control learned the new task faster in every pair, and the advantage held on different starting models as well as on the larger Qwen3-1.7B. Copies with no reward signal, trained only on the updates that every copy shared, learned about as fast as the yoked copies. The advantage is therefore mostly a benefit of control, not damage from lacking it. Control had also changed how the copies answered, so the twins practiced different answers. That practice could carry part of the advantage, and Experiment 2 removed the difference. Both copies of a pair trained on the same answers, fixed in advance, in the same order, and received the same number of rewards. Only one copy's rewards followed the answers, and that copy again learned a new task faster. The advantage of the copies with control over their yoked twins could be forecast before the new task began from each copy's weights. In sum, control over rewards during earlier training left models faster at learning a new task later on, and a conventional model evaluation need not show it.

title: Do Visual RL Gains Scale at Test Time? A Quantile View of Post-Training
authors: Austin Wang, Lexing Ying
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the single-sample quality of visual generative models, but deployment often provides additional inference compute through Best-of-N sampling. Whether RL gains transfer under such test-time scaling, particularly on difficult held-out tasks, remains poorly understood in the visual domain. Our central contribution is to systematically identify and characterize a failure mode of scaling transfer in visual RL: across multiple RL methods, model backbones, and evaluations spanning compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, higher single-sample reward does not necessarily imply a better quality-compute frontier. RL gains may attenuate, saturate, or even reverse at large sampling budgets, with the base model eventually outperforming its post-trained counterpart. We explain these regimes through a quantile-transfer framework, showing that Best-of-N places increasing weight on the upper tail of the reward distribution as N grows. Consequently, RL can improve typical samples while compressing or degrading the rare high-quality outcomes that test-time scaling exploits. As a simple intervention motivated by this analysis, we introduce Quantile Utility Policy Optimization (QUPO), which optimizes a controllable mixture of quantile utilities corresponding to different inference budgets. Experiments on SD3.5-M and BAGEL show that QUPO better preserves upper-tail quality and substantially improves scaling on challenging held-out prompts relative to standard RL post-training. Our results suggest that visual generative models should be evaluated and optimized not only for single-sample quality, but for how post-training reshapes the full reward distribution that inference-time scaling exploits.

title: Beyond Accuracy: How Quantization Affects Coding Agents
authors: Areej Mehboob, Muhammad Ali Shafique, Muhammad Usman Qadeer, Hamza Farooq
abstract: Agents are increasingly used for coding tasks, but the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) limits where they can run. Quantization reduces model size, but its effects on coding agents that execute and revise programs remain underexplored. We compare BF16 with 4-bit AWQ and GPTQ for Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct (7B, 14B, and 32B) and Devstral-Small-2507 (24B) on OJBench coding problems across three seeds. We detect no statistically significant accuracy loss for any of the coding agents. However, final accuracy can conceal substantial behavioral changes: AWQ reduces Qwen-7B one-shot solves from 17 to 0 while increasing loop-based solves from 10 to 25. All Qwen-32B successes involve tool use, whereas Devstral rarely makes a valid executor call. Failure profiles also differ: Qwen-32B produces far more compilation errors than the smaller Qwen models, rising slightly under quantization, while Devstral's failures shift significantly from runtime errors toward wrong answers and timeouts. These findings indicate that quantization robustness in coding agents should be assessed through solution trajectories, tool use, and failure modes, in addition to final accuracy.

title: Malware Clustering in the Wild: Taxonomy, Challenges, and Evaluation Metrics
authors: Raguvir S, Bojing Li, Prajna Bhandary, Charles Nicholas
abstract: As malware continues to grow in volume, diversity, and sophistication, clustering has emerged as a critical technique for analyzing large malware corpora. Clustering enables the discovery of structural relationships, behavioral patterns, and evolutionary trends, and is widely used to group unknown samples, infer malware family boundaries, and identify novel variants. However, existing research remains fragmented, employing a wide range of clustering techniques with no unified perspective that systematically organizes prior work or clearly identifies gaps in the literature. This survey addresses this gap by organizing previous malware clustering research into seven categories: centroid-based, hierarchical-based, density-based, distribution-based, mixed- type, fuzzy, and AI-driven approaches. In addition, this survey summarizes publicly available malware datasets commonly used in clustering research and examines the feature representations derived from these datasets. Our goal is to clarify the current landscape and outline promising avenues for future research on malware clustering, including how AI-driven methods may shape large-scale and reproducible analysis.

title: Nearest Is Not Safest: Fluid-Antenna Port Selection for Over-the-Air Backpropagation in Urban Multipath
authors: Xianzhong Li, Yuzhi Yang, Tianhao Guo
abstract: Over-the-air backpropagation returns a loss gradient through the reciprocal channel, which requires the return port to see the channel of the forward port. If the terminal moves in between, a fluid antenna system can return through the port nearest to the forward position. In ray-traced Chicago streets, with a pedestrian displacement of about half a wavelength and a street-level base station, this rule reverses 20 percent of the gradients at a port spacing of 0.7 wavelengths and 49 percent at 0.9 wavelengths, while one of the four nearest ports stays aligned in all but 2 and 9 percent. We derive a certificate for the sign of the mean correlation from the second moment of a planar angular spectrum. It reduces to a linear program with three variables and infinitely many constraints, is tight, and holds over a region of second moments. In a static Gaussian model, observations collected along a line cannot tell an angular spectrum from its mirror image, so the sign of the cross moment must come from other information. At unsurveyed positions of the same city, a knowledge map that transports surveyed paths through virtual sources and fits them to the causal channel history lowers the reversal rate at 0.9 wavelengths from 49 to 27 percent. Its gain over the nearest port survived every tested error, while its gain over a geometry rule stayed significant at the tested single-error levels of 5 degrees of phase drift per step and 2 mm of position error but not at the next tested levels. Without any survey, across five cities and ten base stations, the nearest port reverses 37 percent of the returns at 0.9 wavelengths and a rule based on the direction and elevation of the base station 20.5 percent. The multilayer perceptrons we tested did not beat these physical rules by the margin fixed in advance in the primary settings.

title: EviCast: Forecasting Retrieval Gains Through Shared Response Calibration
authors: Yibo Wang, Jisheng Dang, Bimei Wang, Jiongpei Hou, Jingwen Zhao, Wenjun Ma, Fei Shen, Juncheng Li, Meng Wang, Qi Tian, Bin Hu, Tat-Seng Chua
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) extends large language models with external evidence, yet relevant evidence does not ensure that a generator can use it.
